Niccolao Manucci, the Venetian traveler who worked in the Mughal court, has written down the details of Dara Shikoh's death. According to him, upon Dara's capture, Aurangzeb ordered his men to have his head brought up to him and he inspected it thoroughly to ensure that it was Dara indeed. He then further mutilated the head with his sword three times. After which, he ordered the head to be put in a box and presented to his ailing father, Shah Jahan, with clear instructions to be delivered only when the old King sat for his dinner in his prison. The guards were also instructed to inform Shah Jahan that, “King Aurangzeb, your son, sends this plate to let him (Shah Jahan) see that he does not forget him”. Shah Jahan instantly became happy (not knowing what was in store in the box) and uttered, “ Blessed be God that my son still remembers me”. Upon opening the box, Shah Jahan became horrified and fell unconscious.

Prior to his recapture of Kandahar, Shah Abbas had also increased Iran’s sway in the southeast by his annexation of the Makran region (in modern Pakistani Baluchistan) in 1608–09.

15/02/2021, 15:51 - +44 7378 311755: Around 2.6 billion years ago, oxygen was seen as an undesirable waste product by most organisms. It was a toxic waste. However, due to cyanobacteria using a revolutionary technique called photosynthesis, which uses the suns energy and carbon dioxide to create food, oxygen was released as a waste product. Around 95 percent of organisms, to whom oxygen was a waste and toxic, died. Only the unicellular organisms which could use oxygen to create energy to live survived. Almost All life on earth present today is descended from those cyanobacteria. Another side effect was that the use of carbon dioxide reduced the greenhouse effect which resulted in the earth cooling to such an extent that it was covered fully in ice. This was known as ‘snowball earth’ as earth was fully covered in ice. Also, this happened not once but at least thrice in the history of the earth.

It was deemed authentic in 862 by a zoroastrian priest in india. The story begins in khorasan, in the year 645 where a group of zoroastrians decide to leave their place to escape persecution by muslims. They initially settle in hormuz island, but seeing that they couldn’t escape persecution there, they decided to leave iran entirely. They boarded a ship and landed in kathiawar peninsula , India. When they landed, they were summoned by the regional king to explain their landing. A group of priests were sent as the representatives of the families who landed. They told the king their story and asked him for asylum. The maharaja was sympathetic to them but explained that his kingdom was already overpopulated and couldn’t sustain them as refugees. He demonstrated this by using a jar of milk completely and said that it will overflow if extra milk is added to it. A zoroastrian priest carefully listened to this and added a teaspoon of sugar to the milk jar, explaining how the sugar brought sweetness to the milk, we will also bring prosperity to the society and not a liability to the population. The king was pleased and impressed by this, but set some conditions, which were  -
1) zoroastrians hand in all their weapons before settling 
2) they adhere to native clothing.
3) adopt gujurati as their mother tongue
4) marry only on evenings.
They readily accepted all the conditions and the parsee community of india came into being.

24/02/2021, 13:44 - +91 81601 63689: In indian context, we have  basically two types of tribes -

1) Non pvtg
2) pvtg

As far as "definition" of tribe is concerned, its very difficult to put forth because every tribe is unique. 

Still, some "culture traits" can be used to classify a group as tribal. These are -

1) lack or very lose form of social gradation. 
2) cohesiveness 
3) intent or severe lack of it to integrate (to sanskritise or convert readily to fight till death)
4) less use of technology
5) attachment to spiritual beliefs (gassains)
6) concentration in a particular geographical location
7) traditional way of life
8) traditional cusine
9) often distinct and premitive farming techniques and tools
10) lesser education
11) shyness in mingling with others
12) more freedom to women



Ofcojrse thers can be exceptions . But these are some of the basic traits

28/02/2021, 09:37 - +91 79852 08674: Following the coronation of Kharak Singh on 1 September 1839, Dhian launched a palace coup on 8 October 1839, and assassinated Chet Singh Bajwa, the favourite courtier of the emperor. He imprisoned emperor Kharak, who later died of slow poisoning by lead and mercury. Dhian had spread rumor that the hedonistic emperor intended to sell out the sovereignty of the Sikh empire to the British East India Company.

Dhian then installed the emperor's son Nau Nihal Singh, aged eighteen, to the throne. Thirteen months later, emperor Nau Nihal, died suddenly on 5 November 1840, on the day of his father's funeral. After leaving the funeral pyre, Nau Nihal was knocked unconscious when a stone gate at Lahore Fort collapsed upon him. Dhian had the emperor carried indoors, and barred any visitors, including the emperor's mother Chand Kaur. Eyewitness accounts had initially reported the emperor had minor injuries from the accident, however later the emperor was pronounced dead when Dhian presented the corpse with its head smashed. American colonel Alexander Gardner, who was with Nau Nihal when he was injured, noted that five artillery men carried the emperor into the fort under the orders of Dhian. Two of these men died mysteriously, two asked for leave and never returned, and one inexplicably disappeared.

On 13 January 1841, Sher Singh led a coup against empress Chand Kaur, and after two days of siege and battle, Dhian negotiated a ceasefire, which led to empress Chand's abdication, and Sher succeeding to the throne as emperor. Later, Dhian had the deposed empress's servants changed, who then assassinated Chand in her palace by smashing her head with wooden pikes on 11 June 1842.

Dhian and emperor Sher were both assassinated on 15 September 1843, in a plot led by Ajit Singh Sandhawalia. Dhian was shot and his body cut into pieces. Dhian's son Hira Singh led a counter-coup the next day, and killed the assassins. On 17 September 1843, Hira Singh Dogra, aged 24, succeeded his father as the prime minister, with five year old infant Duleep Singh being crowned emperor.

Dhian's younger brother Suchet Singh Dogra was killed on 27 March 1844, while leading a failed coup against Dhian's son Hira Singh Dogra. Hira himself was assassinated following another coup d'etat led by Sham Singh Atariwala on 21 December 1844. A year later the First Anglo-Sikh War broke out on 11 December 1845.

28/02/2021, 09:38 - Harshdeep Sir: Well Battle of Attock (9 July, 1813) is known as Panipat of Sikhs,  

Durrani- 15k (11k cavalry, 4k Infantry) Artillery present but not used.

Sikhs- 10k, (8k Cavalry, 2k infantry) Artillery present but used. 

Durrani commander- Wazir Fetah Khan (prime minister of Durrani Empire).

Sikh commander- Dewan Mohkam Chand (commander in chief of Sikh army).

Battle formation- 

Durrani- strong advanced guard under Dost Mohammad Khan on front with Cavalry, center and rearguard under Wazir Fetah Khan, left wing and right wing under Afghan Sardar.

Sikh- 4k Ghorchurras(Sikh Cavalry) divided in two two divisions on right, 4k Ghorchurras(Sikh Cavalry) divided in two divisions on left, Dewan in center on Elephant with 2k infantry of Fauj-i-Ain, very few light Artillery on front under Dewan, major artillery crop in under Ghaus Khan in rear. 

Phase 1. Ghazis charge on front of Sikhs but met with heavy Volley firing, the  Dost Mohammad send Cavalry and was able to force Sikh Infantry on retreat. 

Phase 2. Dewan Mohkam Chand orders Ghaus Khan to fire his Artillery but Ghaus ignored the command, Diwan ordered Ghaus Khan's assistants Aziz Khan and Shaikh Budha to discharge their artillery but Ghaus Khan prohibited them from firing. 

Phase 3. Dewan now within a minute dismounts from his Elephant, take a horse and orders light Artillery to fire and Afghan center is devastated, Sikh Ghorchurras now engaged the Afghan left and right by dismounting, Heavy close quarter combat took place on left and right wing, Dewan now take offensive on center and command a rush on center of Afghans with the help of Sikh infantry. 

Wazir lost the battle and don't dare to risk his rearguard, Afghan survivors escaped on flotilla of boats which was kept ready. The survivors escaped to Khairabad, and many men and horses were drowned in the Indus.

28/02/2021, 18:58 - +91 79852 08674: In the early modern period, much of Asia from the gates of Constantinople to the shores of Chittagong was straddled by three mighty Muslim empires : the Ottomans in Turkey, the Safavids in Persia, and the Mughals in India. Diplomatic excahnges between these three great powers were maintained throughout : more so, between the Safavids and the Mughals. Inspite of their sectarian differences and the occasional scuffles over the Qandahar issue, the Mughals mainatained, by and large, a cordial relation with the Safavid court at Tabriz. Perhaps, the Mughal emperors could never forget the timely assistance their ancestors received at the hands of Shah Ismail and Shah Tahmasp.

After deposing his father and doing away with his brothers, when Aurangzeb ascended the Mughal throne and assumed the imperial title of Alamgir Ghazi, in keeping with the ancient custom, the reigning Persian monarch Shah Abbas II despatched envoys to Delhi to congratulate the new Mughal emperor. However, right from the outset, the relationship between the two kings was not particularly cordial : Aurangzeb could never forget that the Persian king had been a partisan of Murad Baksh; likewise, Aurangzeb's act of usurping the throne while his father was still alive didn't go down well with Shah Abbas II.

The hostility finally spilled over when Tarbiyat Khan, the Subedar of Multan and Mughal ambassador to the Persian court, was given congé by Shah Abbas II and entrusted with an insulting letter meant for Aurangzeb. Here is how the relevant section of the letter reads :

"I learn that most of the chieftains of India are in rebellion because the Mughal ruler is weak, incompetent and without resources. The chief of them is the impious  Shiva, who had long lived in such obscurity that none knew his name; but now, taking advantage of your lack of means and the retreat of your troops, he has made himself visible like the peak of a mighty mountain, seized many forts, slain many of your soldiers, occupied much of your country, plundered many of your ports, cities and villages, and finally wants to come to grips with you! You style yourself a World Conqueror while you have only conquered your father and have gained composure of mind by murdering your brothers."

That Shivaji wasn't an ordinary rebel or a mere regional ruler is clearly borne out by this letter. It was written months before Shivaji's daring escape from Agra, and several years before his audacious attack on Surat. It was natural that the news of these two adventurous feats should have made it to Tabrizi : but the fact that Shivaji's fame had reached the farthest corner of the Islamic world so early on in his career is an eloquent testimony to the kind of legendary status he had earned for himself in his lifetime.

* Extracts of the letter have been reproduced in both Sir Jadunath Sarkar and Riazul Islam's works. It has been put up on the page from the same source. *

This happened in early 1987. So Sundarji had shown that he was the panga taking type much before the IPKF was created for Sri Lanka.

A fascinating figure of our post independence history.

As a young second lieutenant he had stood beside the body of Mahatma Gandhi when it lay in state for 24 hours without a break because the commander forgot to relieve him. 

As a General he created the Mechanised Infantry regiment - thus bringing to  fruition his fascination with tanks even though he was an infantry man. As a major general he was the first infantry officer to command an armoured division. 

As a Lt Gen commanding the College of Combat Mhow (presently the Army War College Mhow) he had written papers in which he had proposed using low kiloton nuclear weapons against enemies if needed. That revolutionized warfare in South Asia. 

Studying his career gives us a deep look  into the post independence military history of India.

07/03/2021, 22:08 - +91 73493 65784: It is one of the greatest mysteries in study of history but underrated

Several different dates have been proposed for Shankaracharyaji:

a) 509–477 BCE: This dating, is based on records of the heads of the Shankara's institutions at Dvaraka Pitha, the Govardhana matha and Badri matha and the Kanchi matha.

b) 44–12 BCE: Anandagiri believed he was born at Chidambaram in 44 BCE and died in 12 BCE.

c) 6th century CE: Telang placed him in this century. Sir R.G. Bhandarkar believed he was born in 680 CE.

d) c. 700 – c. 750 CE: Late 20th-century and early 21st-century scholarship place Shankara's life of 32 years in the first half of the 8th century.

e) 788–820 CE: This was proposed by early 20th scholars and was customarily accepted by scholars such as Max Müller, Macdonnel, Pathok, Deussen and Radhakrishna. The 788–820 CE dates was famous in 20th-century publications but recent scholarship has questioned it.

The popularly-accepted dating places Shankaracharyaji belonging to first half of the 8th century CE.

10/03/2021, 14:02 - +91 73493 65784: His reign was the last nail.

Even before rise of the Shah Mir dynasty, Islam had already spread roots in Kashmir. During the rule of earlier kings, many Shia muslims and Sufi saints had seeked refuge in Kashmir. Shah Mir's ancestors were among those refugees.

After the fall of the Lohara dynasty, Rinchana, a Tibetan Buddhist refugee, became king. He apparently converted to Islam on the advice of his minister Shah Mir as the king lacked the support of Hindus and therefore needed the support of the Kashmiri Muslims. Shah Mir then overthrew Rinchana's successor and secured Muslim rule under his dynasty in Kashmir.
10/03/2021, 14:09 - +91 73493 65784: In the early days of Shah Mir dynasty, there was peace with the occasional communal violence. Sheikh Nooruddin Noorani even combined elements of Kashmir Shaivism with Sufism.

But then things changed. First, Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani arrived in Kashmir and started converting people in large numbers, a good portion of it forcefully.

His follower, Sultan Sikandar, imposed taxes on non–Muslims, forced conversions to Islam, and earned the title Butshikan for destroying idols.
10/03/2021, 14:11 - +91 73493 65784: Hamadani cites 20 edicts for non-Muslims in his book Zakhirat ul Muluk:

1. They will not construct a new temple, church, shrine or a house for idols in that country which is governed by a Muslim ruler.

2. When such places of worship fall to ruin, these should not be re-built.

3. Muslim travellers be disallowed to lodge in churches and temples.

4. They should desist from providing food to a Muslim for three days, should one have to stay in their house.

5. They should not act as spies in a Muslim country and should not provide space to spies in their houses.

6. If their relatives incline to Islam, they should not stop them.

7. They should respect Muslims.

8. If they are sitting at a gathering, they should vacate their place to Muslims entering.

9.They should not dress up like Muslims.

10. They should not adopt for themselves Muslim names.

11. They should not ride horses with saddles and reins.

12. They should not move about with sword and bow and arrow.

13. They should not wear rings with precious stones and those fitted with signets.

14. They should not sell wine nor offer it publicly.

15. They should not give up wearing dresses of pre-Islamic times which they have so that a distinction is maintained between them and Muslims.

16. They should not display traditions and rites of non-Muslims among Muslims.

17. They should not build houses in Muslim neighbourhood.

18. They should not carry their dead near burial places of Muslims.

19. They should not raise their voice mourning their dead.

20. They should not buy Muslim slaves.

Hamadani further states that if any non-Muslims violates any of the above conditions then they forfeit their rights to life and property and those may be rightfully taken away by Muslims as though they were captured infidels.

16/03/2021, 15:23 - Vaibhav: Kshatriya clans mentioned in the sacred books, the Puranas, and in the two great Indian epics are classified into three basic lineages :

1) Suryavanshi:

or Raghuvanshies (the clans of the Solar dynasty), descended through Manu, Ikshvaku, Harischandra, Raghu, Dasaratha and Rama.

2) Chandravanshi:

or Somavanshies (the clans of the lunar dynasty), descended through Yayati, Deva Nausha, Puru, Yadu, Kuru, Pandu, Yudhisthira and Krishna.
The Yaduvanshi lineage are a major sub-branch of the Chandravanshi lineage. Lord Krishna was born a Yaduvanshi.
The Puruvanshi lineage are a major sub-branch of the Chandravanshi Rajputs. The Kauravs and Pandavs of the epic Mahabharata were Puruvanshis.

3) Agnivanshi:

The Agniculas (the clans of the fire dynasty), descended from Agnipala, Swatcha, Mallan, Gulunsur, Ajpala and Dola Rai.
Each of these Vanshas or lineages is divided into several clans (kula), all of whom claim direct patrilineage from a remote but common male ancestor who supposedly belonged to that Vansha. Some of these 36 main clans are further subdivided into shakhas or “branches”, again based on the same principle of patrilineage.

19/03/2021, 16:10 - Vaibhav: The history of Assam can be divided into four eras. The ancient era began in the 4th century with the mention of Kamarupa in Samudragupta's inscriptions on the Allahabad pillar and the establishment of the Kamarupa kingdom. The medieval era began with the attacks from the Bengal Sultanate, the first of which took place in 1206 by Bakhtiyar Khilji as mentioned in the Kanai-boroxiboa rock inscription, after the breakup of the ancient kingdom and the sprouting of medieval kingdoms and chieftain-ships in its place. The colonial era began with the establishment of British control after the Treaty of Yandaboo in 1826, and the post-colonial era began in 1947 after the Independence of India.

Despite this advantage. The Indian swordsman of 18-19 cen were generally able to beat European soldiers when they wielded swords. This proves the immense skill gap between the two, European infantry had heavily decreased using swords and only saw it as a backup weapon or a showpiece for officers
The cavalry did use swords but didn't duel much and just did hit and run with their swords thus losing a massed melee encounter

While Indian and afghans still saw the sword as the noblest weapon that defined ones strength and skill and this trained earnestly

The areas of Assam (Northeast in general, Burma etc) have very dense forests and there is barely any open field for battle.
In such confined spaces, smaller and shorter blades are far more lethal than the longer rapiers (which become hard to wield).

Shorter blades have their own importance. The forested /hilly regions have a range of shorter, but potent blades.

These may not be any match to the longer swords and spears in an open battlefield in plains. But when they are in their own territory, these outclass the traditional weapons.

24/03/2021, 17:14 - +91 96170 36172: Chhatri of Malhar Rao Holkar at Alampur in Bhind, Madhya Pradesh. 

Alampur was a small, isolated pargana belonging to Indore State but situated in the Bundelkhand Agency, Central India, with an area of 37 square miles, lying round the town of Alampur.

 The pargana was formed in 1766 when Malhar Rao Holkar, the founder of the Kingdom of Indore, died suddenly at the village of Alampur. To provide for the upkeep of his last resting place, 27 villages were obtained from the neighbouring chiefs of Gwalior, Datia, Jalaun, and Jhansi, and their revenues devoted to this purpose. The Rajput chiefs, from whom the villages were probably taken by force, were long opposed to the erection of the dead Maharaja's cenotaph, and destroyed it several times. Finally, however, with the support of Sindhia the work was completed. The pargana was managed directly from Indore, the largest being Alampur, also called Malharnagar.

http://yogeshmp.blogspot.com/2017/07/malhar-rao-holkar-at-alampur-in-bhind.html

28/03/2021, 01:11 - +44 7378 311755: Why did Alexander the great not pursue his conquests beyond Uzbekistan?
28/03/2021, 03:20 - Vaibhav: Alexander the Great spent around two years in Uzbekistan during his conquest of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. He experienced there not just some of the most difficult fighting of the entire campaign, but also some of the most remarkable events of his expedition into Asia.

Through 330bc, Alexander had chased the Persian nobleman Bessus around Afghanistan. Bessus was leading the Persian resistance to Alexander, and Alexander had to capture him to ensure the complete submission of the Persian Empire. In 329bc, Alexander crossed the Oxus after leaving the Afghan city of Balkh, and was shortly able to get hold of Bessus, who was sent off for execution. However, Alexander remained in the region to consolidate his power. Perhaps foolishly, he did not make use of his natural allies in the region. Shortly after crossing the Oxus he discovered a town that was inhabited by Greeks, who welcomed him wholeheartedly. However, on discovering that they had collaborated with the Persians when they had invaded Greece in 480bc, he executed the entire settlement and levelled it to the ground. Proceeding northward, he captured Samarkand and then reached the Syr Darya (River Jaxartes) where he founded Alexandria Eschate, 'Alexandria-the-Farthest', modern-day Khojend in Tajikistan.

Despite this immediate success, there was considerable disquiet in the area. Alexander faced a number of uprisings from the indigenous Sogdians and Scythian tribesmen. They were able to employ guerrilla hit-and-run tactics again Alexander, relying on their mastery of horsemanship and archery to strike at his columns from a distance. Alexander had not faced this sort of warfare before, and he had to develop new tactics to defeat the nomadic warriors, including the combined use of catapults and archers, as well as hunting his opponents down to their fortresses and carrying out a conventional campaign of sieges. Despite being badly injured and suffering from dysentery, Alexander was able to lead his men to a notable success against the Scythians on the Syr Darya River.

As Alexander gained the upper hand, his opponents rallied at a fortress called the Sogdian Rock on top of a large escarpment. Its site is not known for certain, but it is thought to be near Samarkand. They thought it impregnable, and taunted Alexander that he would need soldiers with wings to capture it. Alexander was so irked by their jibes that he called for volunteers to scale the sheer cliffs up to the fortress. Three hundred men came forward and, using ropes and tent pegs, they made the ascent in the dead of night. Although 30 were lost in the climb, by morning they were inside the fortress. Alexander's herald shouted that they had found the soldiers with wings, and the defenders, amazed, surrendered immediately.

According to Greek historians, Alexander met on the rock a princess named Roxane, the daughter of one of the local rulers, Oxyartes. They record that he fell in love with her on sight and arranged a marriage with her. Having made such an alliance, he was ready to proceed out of Uzbek lands on his attempt to conquer India. The legend of Roxane still lives today, and many distinguished families in the region claim descent from the union of Alexander and Roxane.

28/03/2021, 11:55 - +91 91657 26016: *The Battle of Gaugamela* 

also called the Battle of Arbela was the decisive battle of Alexander the Great's invasion of the Persian Achaemenid Empire. In 331 BC Alexander's army of the Hellenic League met the Persian army of Darius III near Gaugamela, close to the modern city of Dohuk  in Iraqi Kurdistan. Though heavily outnumbered, Alexander emerged victorious due to his army's superior tactics and his deft employment of light infantry. It was a decisive victory for the Hellenic League and led to the fall of the Achaemenid Empire.

These factors give context, content, and set the conditions and parameters in which an economy functions. 08/04/2021, 12:34 - Vaibhav: Most bows were made from yew but ash, hazel and elm. The string of the bow was made from hemp or strong plant fibers like that of Agarvee as it was the strongest and least elastic fibre available. The string was then soaked in  plant glue as some protection against moisture.

Then the bow was covered with a soft layer of wood which was optional and not very much there in the world. Then leather grips were attached to it wherein the grip was cut in a line from the middle. Then,  it was positioned and stitched.

This was how a Bow was made..

18/04/2021, 16:44 - +91 73493 65784: To understand y Mussolini planned and executed the March on Rome, we have to go back before the start of WW1.

Mussolini was initially a Socialist and ardent follower of Italian and even German socialists. He was fierce anti imperialist and pro pacifist guy.

But his views started to change to Nietzche's Ubermensch rejecting religion and egalitarianism.

When WW1 broke out, he supported the decision of the Italian Socialist Party of not participating in the war. But like many other socialists, he saw this war as a chance to overthrow the 'imperial' powers of Europe and start a revolutionary war.

Therefore he changed his stance to pro war and was subsequently expelled from the party. This radically transformed Mussolini's ideology from class conflict to Revolutionary Nationalism. He formed the Fascio Rivoluzionario d'Azione Internazionalista and started to  attract people from all over the spectrum.

After the end of war, he was convinced that Socialism was a failure and Italy needed to be radicalized. He slowly turned to the possibility of using war to expand the borders of Italy like that of the Roman Empire and was convinced of Italy's destiny to rule Mediterranean.

He then formed the National Fascist Party which was seen as a Third way as opposed to conservatives and socialists. The party expanded quickly attracting war veterans, disgruntled socialists, Italian supremacists, etc.

In the night between 27 and 28 October 1922, 30,000 Blackshirts (the military arm of the Fascists) gathered in Rome and demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Luigi Facta and the appointment of a new government under Mussolini. King Victor Emmanuel III refused the government request to declare martial law as he feared the possibility of Civil War as the country was already in crisis. This led to Facta's resignation and the King then handed over power to Mussolini by asking him to form a new government.

In 1908, during the excavations at the Shah-ji-ki-Dheri mound in Peshawar, archaeologist DB Spooner found a small gilded bronze casket with a tightly fitted lid, sitting on a coin issued during the reign of the Kushana Emperor Kanishka. This was deceptively simple for something that once held the relics of the Buddha.⠀
⠀
On the lid of the casket were etchings of the Buddha surrounded by the Vedic deities Indra and Brahma. On the edge of the lid, a frieze of geese in flight, a very Greek motif. The casket as a whole displays many features of Greek art that are typical also of Gandhara art, and the Gandhara region where it was found.

🔴In linguistics, MUTUAL INTELLIGIBILITY is a  relationship between languages or dialects in which speakers of different but related varieties can readily understand each other without prior familiarity or special effort for example under Punjabi Language a Doabi dialect speaker can fully understand Majhi dialect speaker.

🔴 In map you can see nearly 35 to 40 languages and almost all of them are not mutually intelligible with Hindi Language nor they have  same origin history as of Hindi Language so how Indian Government can make them dialect of Hindi Language ?

🔴 First of all, I would like to talk about Bihari Group that includes Bhojpuri, Magahi, Maithili, Sadri, Khortha, Vajjika, Angika,Tharu and Panch Pargania. Bihari Languages are not mutually intelligible with Hindi. Bihari Group Language uses Kaithi and Tirhuta Script for writing purpose. This Bihari Group along with Assamese, Bengali and Odia have its origin from Magadhi Prakrit Language and Hindi has origin from Shauraseni Prakrit. So, how a group of languages having totally different origin history and script can be tagged as dialect of Hindi by Ind Govt.

🔴 Secondly, I would like to talk about Rajasthani Group Languages which include Marwari, Mewari, Hadoti, Dhundari, Malvi Nimadi,Bagri, Shekhawati, Mewati, Ahirwati, Godwadi and Dhatki . Rajasthani Languages are not mutually intelligible with Hindi Language though Rajasthani and Hindi both have their origin from Shauraseni Prakrit Language but still they both are not intelligible with each other. Moreover, Rajasthani Languages have its own Mahajani Script for writing and has literary works.  Rajasthani is Indo Aryan Language of Western Zone and Hindi is Indo Aryan Language of Central Zone. So how a language can be dialect of language of totally different zone ? 

🔴 Thirdly, I want to talk about Western Pahari and Central Pahari Languages. Western Pahari include Himachali, Bhadarwahi, Padari and Jaunsari. Whereas Central Pahari includes Garhwali and Kumaoni. They have their own script i.e Takri and have written literary works .They are not mutually intelligible with Hindi. These Pahari Languages are Indo Aryan Languages of North Zone and Hindi is Indo Aryan Language of Central Zone.  So, these Pahari Languages are not dialect of Hindi.

🔴 Now lets discuss about Eastern Hindi group languages. This group includes 5 languages i.e Awadhi, Bagheli, Powari, Surgujia and Chattisgarhi. This group name is now officially changed from Eastern Hindi Group to Kosali Group because though this group has Hindi in its name but languages of this group are not mutually intelligible with Hindi Language. Languages of this group uses Kaithi Script for writing purpose and have their own literary works. Moreover, languages of Eastern Hindi Group (now Kosali Group) had its origin from Ardhmagadhi Prakrit and Hindi has its origin from Shauraseni Prakrit. So, how a group of languages with different origin history can be dialect of Hindi ?

🔴 Now lets discuss about Western Hindi group of Languages which includes Haryanvi, Khadi, Braj Bhasha, Kannauji and Bundeli. By the way, only Khadi can be considered as dialect of Hindi because it gave birth to Hindi and Urdu. But other 4 languages i.e Haryanvi, Braj Bhasha, Kannauji and Bundeli cannot be called dialect of Hindi. As they are not intelligible with Hindi Language though they are considered most closer to Hindi and have similar origin from Shauraseni Prakrit. They have their own script and literary works Haryanvi and Bundeli has Langdi Script and its own literary work. Most of the bhajans and aartis of Lords of Hindu Region (Sanatan) are written in Kannauji and Braj Bhasha.  

🔴 Surjapuri Language which is a Indo Aryan Language of Bengali - Assamese variety is not at all mutually intelligible with Hindi language and have different history of origin, scripts , etc . 20/05/2021, 10:20 - Vaibhav: Sure, I'll tell what I remember,

History of Camera starts from all the way to 11nth century wherein the camera was in a big box and required to be in a dark room just like when we see a ray of light in a dark room. Scientifically speaking the process is Natural Optical Illusion. Han Chinese were the first to discover it as may researchers say. This camera didn't hadodern camera but was more of like a telescope or so..

In 17nth century, The pinhole camera was discovered wherein lenses were used to see the inverted image.

In the 1830's Henry Fox made a new camera with a substance called as silver salts to protect it from sunlight and other natural phenomenon affecting the photograph.

The first photographic camera developed for commercial manufacture was a durable  camera, built by Alphonse Giroux in 1839.   The cameras were produced in France.

In 1810's a new camera was Made to control the amount of sunlight to pass to lens. Then the pretzel lens were used which were 30 times faster than regular ones.

In 1885, paper first made its way in Camera world. Then paper was intermixed or so with the other observations and findings and so we had a photography paper camera. The paper was different too..

As technology advances the camera also advanced.

It was all about one-upmanship from Soviet and US regimes.

They went to extra-ordinary lengths in all fields (not just military) to showcase themselves as better than the other.

The one-upmansip with Russia still continues but it is not as vitriolic as it was during the height of cold war.

The cold war was evident in scientific field, sports, humanitarian aid, international relations.....

26/05/2021, 16:28 - Vaibhav: Kathak is derived from the sanskrit word 'Katha' or story. Yes from South to North it moved. 

First, Kathak was seen as a storytelling part wherein people recited stories mostly linked with Hinduism.

Kathak was only forbidden to temples under the Cholas and other South Indian Dynasties like that of Pallava, Pandyas. 

Later Kathak had a major reform wherein the story would be deducted by movement of legs, angles of hands, and vibrations of Ghungrus and Payals. Then the dancers danced and at the same time, storytellers recited.

However, it was not a good way as viewers found it difficult to focus on both the dance and the story. And so it was changed to only dance.

This reform also provided Kathak to be performed at special training houses, Temples and Courts. Also now womens could performed it in groups.

When it came to North, Kathak was like an addiction. Courts began to patronize Kathak. The addiction was so wild that Kathak schools were formed.

There were Kathak Schools all over India but the most prominent one was the Luckhnowi Gharana and the Benaras Gharana.

Kathak saw a bit of droppings in the East India Company Reign. 

However, under the last Nawab of Awadh Wasjid Ali Shah, Kathak flourished in Awadh.

Today, Kathak is widely known for it's popularity in the north it's hard moves and techniques and Kathak Dances are very much respected in India as far I have seen.

Respect to all Kathak Masters..

26/05/2021, 22:13 - Vaibhav: Core beliefs of Buddhism according to Gautam Buddha-

1) Death is inevitable and no mortal can stop death.

2)  Avoiding Ignorance is very important to find the right path.

3) Every problem, Illness, Life and Death is due to the will or expectations or 'Icha' ( in hindi).

4) 'Icha' should be excluded forever to get rid of all the tensions, problems and bad things in life.

5) Everyone should follow thier path and follow thier respective duties.

6) Don't be mean and cruel, help others and be nice.

7) Control your mind, reflexes and other organs to follow the path.

06/06/2021, 22:09 - +91 73493 65784: Savarkar was a revolutionary since his teens. He was part of the Swadeshi movement during his college days in Pune. He and his brother found an underground society called Abhinav Bharat Society.

He then went to Britain to pursue his law studies. In Britain he stayed at India House, gathering place for Indian Revolutionaries and also joined Free India Society.

He was the first prominent India to call the Revolt of 1857 as the Indian War for Independence (which the British called a Mutiny). The book was banned by the British.

He smuggled arms and ammunition through books. He was arrested by the British in 1910 for Revolutionary activities related to Indian House.

He was sent back to India but escaped from the ship to France. But the French returned him back to the British.

In India, he was sentenced to 50 years of imprisonment and hard labour to Kaala Pani for crimes against His Majesty's Government. One of the heaviest sentences of the British era.

06/06/2021, 22:13 - +91 73493 65784: Savarkar's arrest at Marseilles caused the French government to protest against the British, arguing that the British could not recover Savarkar unless they took appropriate legal proceedings for his rendition. The dispute came before the Permanent Court of International Arbitration in 1910, and it gave its decision in 1911. The case excited much controversy as was reported widely by the French press, and it considered it involved an interesting international question of the right of asylum.

The Court held, firstly, that since there was a pattern of collaboration between the two countries regarding the possibility of Savarkar's escape in Marseilles and there was neither force nor fraud in inducing the French authorities to return Savarkar to them, the British authorities did not have to hand him back to the French for the latter to hold rendition proceedings. On the other hand, the tribunal also observed that there had been an "irregularity" in Savarkar's arrest and delivery over to the Indian Army Military Police guard.

While the Ghurids were busy fighting other Hindu dynasties such as the Gahadavalas, Hariraja once again invaded Ajmer in 1193 CE. This time, he managed to recapture Ajmer, and became the new Chauhan king, with support from Prithviraja's former general Skanda. Hariraja also sent a force under Jatira to capture Delhi. However, the force had to retreat in fear of a larger Ghurid army. As Jatira's force was returning to Delhi, Hariraja set out from Ajmer with another army in its support. The Ghurids decisively defeated the Chauhan forces in the subsequent battle.

According to the 16th century Muslim historian Ferishta, Hariraja and Jaitra were killed in this battle. However, Taj-ul-Maasir, which was written just after this period, states that Jaitra "sacrificed himself in the flames of a fire". Hammira Mahakavya by the Jain scholar Nayacandra Suri also states that Hariraja had to fall back to Ajmer, where he determined that any further resistance against the Ghurids was fruitless and as a result, he and his family committed suicide by self-immolation.

17/07/2021, 19:30 - +91 63065 04255: Capitalism is often thought of as an economic system in which private actors own and control property in accord with their interests, and demand and supply freely set prices in markets in a way that can serve the best interests of society.

The essential feature of capitalism is the motive to make a profit. As Adam Smith, the 18th century philosopher and father of modern economics, said: “It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.” Both parties to a voluntary exchange transaction have their own interest in the outcome, but neither can obtain what he or she wants without addressing what the other wants. It is this rational self-interest that can lead to economic prosperity.

In a capitalist economy, capital assets—such as factories, mines, and railroads—can be privately owned and controlled, labor is purchased for money wages, capital gains accrue to private owners, and prices allocate capital and labor between competing uses.

Although some form of capitalism is the basis for nearly all economies today, for much of the last century it was but one of two major approaches to economic organization. In the other, socialism, the state owns the means of production, and state-owned enterprises seek to maximize social good rather than profits

03/08/2021, 11:13 - +91 73493 65784: It depends on the balance of power between the two sides.

If one country is stronger than the other, it can dictate terms or even force them to accept it, eg:- Treaty of Versailles (1919) and Treaty of Frankfurt (1872)

If both are on equal terms, then the methods of negotiations depends on whether they are fighting or not. During peace times, they would exchange gifts, solve disputes through their respective diplomats, scheme behind the scenes, demand compensation if any damages were caused to trading vessels or caravans, etc.

During war time, the role of diplomats and time becomes really crucial as the delay of terms can delay a peace treaty.

14/08/2021, 22:39 - Vaibhav: Some reasons that I can share-

1) World War I -

World War I was disastrous for Britain. Britain was literally emptying it's coffers for the allies to hold the Central Powers. Several wars literally emptied the British coffers. Battles like- Battle of Somme, Battle of Verdun, Allies at Gallipolli, Ottoman Empire etc. Same was with France. Britain's GDP was falling hard and Britain had to look for a solution for the falling economy. And the answer was India and other colonies. Britain was saved indirectly by India from the economic catastrophe after ww1.

2) World War II -

It was the major reason for the downfall of Great Britain.   After Hitler used blitzkrieg against the allies, Britain made a desperate escape at Dunkirk but they left the war supplies. According to Hitler's plan,Britain was starving and cities got heavy damage. It was said that Britain was literally about to give up and was fully dependent upon United States of America and the Soviet Union. We know about Britain's condition so we can imagine that the economy must be so much affected. Even the colonies refused to help Britain. India however helped a bit but wanted independence in return which Britain had to give. This shows that Britiah economy was crumbling in the World Wars.

3) Rise of America and the Soviet Union-

Since America was trading with Britain, it became super rich and eventually after WW2, became a global superpower both in terms of economy and technology. America especially after WW II had replaced Britain and became the dominant power of the west.

Soviet Union were the next. The rise of USSR was a nightmare for Britain. USSR had got the eastern block as the reward for the victory in WW2. This boosted the Soviet Economy and other reasons were also there. The Soviet Union replaced Britain as the dominant power in Europe. Britain also joined NATO as its economic condition was so bad that people couldn't even afford daily food and industries were also destroyed.

4) Colonies-

Britain had to grant independence to its colonies that greatly reduced Britain's economy. 

These were some reasons for Britain's downfall.

22/08/2021, 12:46 - +91 99679 76550: There are 3 main sources:

1. Chhatrasal Dashak
2. Chhatra Prakash
3. Chhatrasal's letters

The first two are contemporary poetic accounts and have poetic exaggerations. The third source is correspondence of Chhatrasal himself. He wrote some accounts of his early battles upon his son's request. Some of these accounts are also prone to exaggeration.

However, Chhatrasal's rebellion was not a single war, but rather a gradual process. He started off with some 25-30 people with him, when he left Shivaji's camp. He tried to rally other Bundelas to his cause, but there was not much support. However, Aurangzeb's temple demolition orders, especially his move towards Orchha helped turn the tide. Chhatrasal became a central figure in this and carved a major territory for himself.

The other part of this story is that he was not fully out of Mughal administration. He went in and out and occasionally even participated in the campaigns against Marathas and Sikhs.

25/08/2021, 17:50 - +91 73493 65784: A women used to take their husband's surname in Europe due to financial, heritence and identity factors.

For example, a noble woman kept her brith surname as it had value and claim to her ancestral lands or wealth. Common women generally had no land attached to their original surname and therefore took their husbands surname to avoid legal problems (generally the common people who had surnames were of upper middle or middle class, the lower class rarely used surnames in Medieval Period).

Considering that Darwin's theory of evolution holds for humans, the concept of communicating with each other was inherited from ape ancestors (they have their own peculiar methods for communicating), and it kept on developing through various newer species until homosapiens came up. 04/10/2021, 08:55 - +91 81444 90555: The story I wish to share is About the word "Burmah" you see in the photo and the hsistory behind "Digbot" and its petroleum, reserve
04/10/2021, 08:56 - +91 81444 90555: Its about part of the history of this place named Digboi in Assam. The oldest refinery in the world which is still functioning. The story of oil exploration in India began in the dense jungles and swamps and river-valleys of the north-eastern corner of the country. Lt. R. Wilcox, Major A. White, Capt. Francis Jenkins, Capt. P.S. Hanny, W. Griffith, W.Licut Bigge–they all saw at different times petroleum seepages from the banks of river Dihing. Mr. C.A Bruce (1828) and Mr. H.B. Medicott (1865) of the Geological survey of India also saw oil seepages while prospecting for coal in upper Assam.

 

Barely seven years after Edwin L. Drake drilled the world's first oil well in 1859 at Titusville, Pennsylvania, USA, in 1866, Mr. Goodenough of McKillop, Stewart and Company, Calcutta, drilled a hand-dug well of 102 feet at Nahorpung near Jaipur area of Upper Assam but failed to establish satisfactory production. In his second attempt on 26 March 1867, oil was struck at merely 118 feet (35.97-m) in Asia's first mechanically drilled well at Makum near Margherita area of Upper Assam. 

 

However, the first well dug at Digboi field in Assam in September 1889  and completed in November 1890 at depth of 662 feet by Assam Railways and Trading Company Limited (AR&T Co. Ltd.), registered at London, is regarded as the first commercially successful oil discovery (200 gallons per day). To add color to geologic reasoning legend was created that during the construction of a railway line by AR&T, in the year 1867, a herd of logging elephants returned to camp with their feet covered in oil after a night time excursion to find food and water. This led men to trail to the salt lick where seepages were prolific. Looking this, the elated English owner cried out to his men, “Dig boy, dig". Probably the name Digboi itself came from that word.

 

AR&T subsequently acquired a 77.7 square kilometer petroleum-rights concession in the Makum area of Assam, and by 1893 had drilled 10 wells at Digboi producing 757.08 liters/day. AR&T established Assam Oil Company (AOC) in 1899 with a capital of £310,000 to take over the petroleum interests of AR&T, including the Digboi and Makum concessions and set up a small refinery at Margharita (Upper Assam) with a capacity of 500 bopd to refine the Digboi-oil. Thereafter, systematic drilling began in 1891 and two years later in 1901, Asia's first oil refinery was set up in at Digboi. It is still functional and world's oldest operating refinery.

 

Failure to utilize geologic reasoning, promiscuous wild catting, misguided investment and nonchalance of the management towards technical support led to compounding of errors by AOC which made the company technically and financially impotent. Later on UK based Burma Oil Company (BOC) arrived in 1911 in Upper Assam (Surma Valley) and in 1915, after acquiring Oil interest from Budderpore Oil Co. Ltd (formed by a syndicate of Budderpore tea garden during 1911-13) began testing option in the Badarpur structure in the Surma valley (Upper Assam). Gradually by 1921, in a phase-wise manner, BOC acquired petroleum interests of AOC.

04/10/2021, 10:33 - +91 99679 76550: A few factors which helped ..

- Human heart is incredibly powerful. It allowed us to run for a long time and chase down an animal with persistence. Early humans were very effective hunters.

- The upright gesture which allowed us to use two limbs for hunting and other tasks, rather than walking. 

- Our walking is a fairly complex function. There's a reason it takes babies a while to learn to walk. When we walk, we are usually just rolling forward and then moving with our feet in such a way that keeps the centre of gravity below us i.e. balancing us. This is a very energy efficient process, in comparison with other animals who have to lift their bodies against gravity to move.

- The opposable thumb, which allows us to grip objects. This has allowed humans to use tools far more efficiently than any other animals. It also allows us to carry stuff, giving us lot more flexibility and advantage over other species.

08/10/2021, 18:05 - +91 88790 53699: Actually how does sword cut? 

That is decided by force per unit length. If it is more the sword is more effective, if it is less sword is less effective for cutting. 


In the straight sword, contact length increases but for curved sword effective contact length decreases. 

So for the same applied force effectiveness of the curved sword increases. Or with less force you can have better effective sword application. 

But you need to have harder material for curved one. 

Also straight sword will be more effective when you want to penetrate.
08/10/2021, 18:10 - +91 88790 53699: <Media omitted>

08/10/2021, 18:14 - +91 74062 38254: The use of the curved and straight swords in cavalry would depend on the function of the respective units, 
For eg. The European cavalry in second half of the 18th century and upto WW1 extensively used straight swords. For most of the time their function was to act as 'shock' troops... (light cavalry) where a unit would charge to break the infantry line formations, to break the order. The idea of using straight sword here is to kill the enemy by piercing by generated momentum... and penetrate deep into enemy formation by virtue of speed.(we can also see in modern day horseman stunts where they demonstrate the similar act called fencing)... heavy cavalry was used for 'flanking' purposes they would use both curved and straight swords. 
On the other hand in India curved blade was popular in medieval times... although cavalry men in ancient south India atleast used also straight swords i can say this because the carvings on the belur channakeshava temple  depicts use of straight swords.
But Indian cavalry men often fought with lances/long spears.

14/10/2021, 19:56 - +91 79997 63794: When JRD Tata was just 25 years old, an interesting news item in the London Times newspaper caught his attention. A unique air race had just been announced, by His Highness The Aga Khan, spiritual leader of the Shia Imami Ismaili Muslims, to popularize aviation and flying in India. The announcement read :

“The Aga Khan has offered through the Royal Aero Club, a prize of UK Pounds 500, for the first flight from England to India, or vice-versa, by a person of Indian nationality. It must be a solo flight, completed within six weeks, from the date of starting. The prize will remain open for one year from 1st January 1930.”

JRD Tata was already an avid flyer, and he had just obtained his flying license earlier that year. Since he was the first person to have qualified in India, his license, issued by the Aero Club of India and Burma, proudly bore the number “1”. He was now excited by the Aga Khan Prize, and decided to take up this flying challenge. India to England, or vice-versa, was an arduous route, with several days of solitary flying over the sultry deserts, swamps and marshes of Iraq, Egypt and Basra. Given the small bi-planes of those years, the race to reach first would also involve several stop-overs along the way.

Two other flyers also decided to take up the challenge, seized by the same excitement as JRD. One of them was Manmohan Singh, an enthusiastic civil engineer with aeronautical training, from Rawalpindi. The second was Aspy Merwan Engineer, a dashing young man who had obtained his flying license at Karachi. So here was a race involving three people. The big question – who would win ?

Manmohan Singh and Aspy Engineer decided to fly from England to India, whereas JRD went the other way around – he began at Karachi, and aimed to reach Croydon airport, in England. Manmohan Singh’s attempts were unfortunately not successful. Once, he got lost in a thick fog in a mountain road in Southern Italy, and his aircraft, which he had interestingly named “Miss India”, was badly damaged. He bravely persevered, but on another attempt, he had to make a forced landing in a swamp near Marseilles, and, while he did eventually reach India, he could not make it in the stipulated time.

In the meanwhile, the second competitor, Aspy Engineer, started out from England, in his second-hand DeHavilland, Gypsy Moth bi-plane, on 25th April 1930. He was only 17 years old.  A superb aviator, he flew very well, but encountered some engine trouble over Libya, at Benghazi, due to faulty spark plugs. Aspy was well known for his mechanical and engineering skills, and so, despite these problems, he was able to reach the Aboukir airstrip, near Alexandria in Egypt. 

Here, Aspy parked his plane, and immediately began his hunt for spark plugs in good condition, which would enable him to fly further. This was not an easy search in this far-flung location, and it could take several days for these spark plugs to reach him. Valuable time would surely be lost.

We now turn our eyes to the third competitor in the flying race, JRD Tata. Where was he? JRD had taken off from Karachi on 3rd May 1930, in a Gyspy Moth G-AAGI plane. He faced significant headwinds as he flew towards Jask, a small, hot and dusty town on the coast of Iran. There, he stayed overnight, and then took off towards Basra in Iraq. He drifted a little, and had to double back from the salt marshes, north of Lingoh, to reach Basra. From Basra, he flew towards Baghdad, and then onwards towards Cairo. 

En route, his faulty compass led him to drift out again, and land in an old, disused First World War airstrip covered in anthills, at Haifa. But he recovered quickly from this error, and reached Cairo, where he was re-directed to land at the Aboukir airstrip. In other words, he had reached the same airport near Alexandria where Aspy Engineer had parked his plane for some time now, searching for the elusive spark plugs which would enable him to resume his race.

What happened at Aboukir that day is beautifully chronicled by JRD Tata’s biographer, RM Lala. Here is what JRD told Lala.

“At Alexandria, at 7am., I saw another Moth parked there and realized it must be Aspy Engineer (my competitor)…When he heard that I had landed, he came out to the aerodrome to meet me. I asked him what he was doing there. He told me he was waiting for some spare plugs, since he had not taken an extra set of them. This was not very good planning ! Since mine was a four-cyclinder aeroplane, and I had eight spare plugs, I gave him four of them. He was so pleased and grateful that he insisted I take something from him, and he have me his Mae West life jacket. He had a Mae West, but no spark plugs!”

So the stranded Aspy Engineer got his spark plugs from his competitor JRD, set his aircraft right, and took off towards India. JRD too got moving quickly, but lost further time in Naples, where he landed late evening at a military airfield. Here, because of strict army rules, he had to wait for the military commandant to permit him to take off, and lost four valuable hours. Thereafter, he flew uneventfully towards Rome and Paris, and then the final leg from Paris to Croydon in England.

However, by the time JRD landed in Paris, Aspy Engineer had already reached Karachi in India, and had won the Aga Khan Prize. JRD Tata had lost the flying competition by just 2 hours and 30 minutes. The race was over.

But wait a moment...that is not the end of this story (as we say in India - Kahaani ab baki hai, mere dost). 27 years later, in 1957, both men had grown significantly in their careers and lives. JRD Tata had become Chairman of the Tata Group, and Aspy Engineer had joined the Indian Air Force, where he had risen to become Air-Vice Marshal. A few years later, Aspy would go on to become the second Indian to head the Indian Air Force.     

Aspy Engineer now wrote to JRD Tata, to greet him on the 25th anniversary of India’s first airline, which JRD had founded way back in 1932. JRD was greatly moved by his letter, and here is an extract from his reply to Aspy, dated 19th October 1957 :

“Of all the letters and messages I have received…none pleased me more or brought back more pleasant memories than yours…Those days were fun, weren’t they ? We were both so much younger, particularly yourself...Although you were only seventeen or eighteen at the time, I atleast did not underestimate you in the Aga Khan competition…I took you so seriously as a competitor that I spent atleast a day more in checking everything on the plane and everything else connected with the trip.”

JRD goes on to say :

“Our friendship ever since has been much more worthwhile than winning the competition would have been. I must say I enjoyed every moment of that adventure as I am sure you did too.”

And then JRD adds a concluding part of the story, in his letter to Aspy :

“Incidentally, one of the highlights that remains imprinted on my memory was my arrival at Karachi by Imperial Airways, on my return to India (from England, after the race). When, to my embarrassment, you met me with a platoon of scouts and presented me with a medal. That was terribly nice of you, and so undeserved.”

So, Aspy Engineer had actually met his competitor JRD on his return, at Karachi airport, and had given him a ceremonial welcome with a platoon, and a special medal too, for helping him win the race. What a graceful gesture, and one that must have surely brought a smile to JRD’s face. And perhaps some tears to his eyes too.

We all run and fly so many races in our lives. Winning some of these races is important to us, but is this all that matters? And is it worthwhile to win them at any cost? Or is it far more important and meaningful, to help someone, to bring a smile to someone’s face, whenever we can, along the way? And to nurture friendships that stand the test of time, which make our lives all the more fulfilling? As we search for our own answers, perhaps we can reflect on this beautiful old story, of JRD Tata and Aspy Engineer, both great men of our nation.

The Festival of the Supreme Being, by Pierre-Antoine Demachy (1794)
27/10/2021, 20:21 - +91 79852 08674: The French revolution had already stripped the Church of its authority and tried to replace Catholicism with the Cult of Reason (an atheist belief system introduced by Robespierre’s rival, Jacques Hébert). But, while Robspierre supported and end to Catholicism, he also believed in the existence of a god. He created a new cult which believed the creation of the universe was an act of a ‘supreme being’ and that human souls are immortal, but that humans are responsible for their own actions and destinies – these are not acts of god. He called this ‘The Cult of the Supreme Being’ and decreed it the new state religion.

This painting shows the Festival of the Supreme Being, a national celebration ordered by and presided over by Robspierre. This lavish event took place on the 8th June 1794 and featured music composed specially for the occasion, a manufactured mountain covered in flowers and a huge papier mâché statue of atheism, specially made by Jacques-Louis David, which was duly set alight.

Many saw this event as the pinnacle of Robspierre’s powers, but by now Robspierre had made many enemies, including among his own followers. Just over a month later, on 28th July, Maximilien Robspierre was overthrown and executed at the guillotine. This not only brought an end to the Reign of Terror but also the Cult of the Supreme Being, which was finally banned along with the Cult of Reason by Napoleon, in 1802.

Fire was always at the disposal of people who lived in extremely cold climates. No one ventured there until they had the wherewithal to combat the bitter cold (fire, clothing, shelter).

During the less cold months the hunting for the entire winter is done. Fish and meat is cut into fine slices and hung up to be dried and smoked. It is then carefully stored for the harsher months to come.
The only fresh stuff that they get is milk and eggs from domesticated animals (if any).

11/11/2021, 13:51 - +91 96170 36172: In 1942, the first group of Navajo code talkers, recruited by the Marine Corps, were tasked with a nearly insurmountable job—coming up with an unbreakable code. Over the course of the war, not one, but two types of code were developed:
 
The first type of code, referred to as “Type One Code” was essentially a simple cypher. Navajo Code Talkers used English words for each letter of the alphabet and then translated these words into their native language. For example, the letter “C” was represented by the English word “cat” and the Navajo word “moasi”. To say “CODE” in Type One Code would be moasi (C-cat), ne-ahs-jah (O-owl), lha-cha-eh (D-dog), dzeh (E-elk). 

Clearly, spelling out words letter by letter would be cumbersome and slow, so a second “Type Two Code” was also developed. This code assigned Navajo words to common pieces of military equipment. For example, “besh-lo” (iron fish) meant “submarine”, “a-ye-shi” (eggs) meant bombs, and “tsidi-ney-ye-hi” (bird carrier) meant aircraft carrier. 
 
Once newly recruited Navajo Code Talkers memorized the codes and competed training, they were sent to Marine units in the Pacific theater where they transmitted coded information over telephones and radios. During the battle for Iwo Jima, six Navajo Code Talkers successfully transmitted more than 800 messages without any errors—a crucial part of the American victory there. 

The Japanese were so perplexed by the Navajo code that it remained unbroken throughout the war. In fact, the code was so successful that it was not de-classified until 1968, meaning that the Navajo Code Talkers who had been so critical to victory, were left without recognition. In 2001, 60 years after the United States entered the Pacific War, Congress awarded Congressional Gold Medals to the Code Talkers. Today, we mark their achievements with National Navajo Code Talkers Day on August 14th. 

Photograph of Navajo Indian Code Talkers Henry Bake and George Kirk courtesy of National Archives

Courtesy National Museum of the Pacific War/ Facebook

13/11/2021, 18:20 - +91 74399 45141: Jagat Seth is a title given to Fateh Chand by the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in 1723. After which this entire family came to be known as Jagat Seth. The founder of this gharana is believed to be Seth Manik Chand. It is said that the ancestors of Jagat Seth Mahtab Rai were residents of Marwar. In 1495 AD, Girdhar Singh Gehlot had accepted Jainism from among the Gehlot Rajputs. Hiranand Sahu of this family left Marwar and settled in Patna in 1652 AD. Patna used to be a big center of trade in those days. Here Hiranand Sahu started the business of saltpetre, in those days Europeans used to be the biggest buyers of saltpetre. Along with the saltpete business, the moneylender had also increased the work of lending on interest and soon he was counted among the rich moneylenders. Hiranand Sahu had seven sons, who were scattered here and there to do business. One of his sons, Manik Chand, came to Dhaka, which was the capital of Bengal at that time.
In fact, it was Manik Chand who had laid the foundation of the Jagat Seth family of Bengal. Murshid Quli Khan Subedar of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and Manik Chand were close friends of each other. Manik Chand was not only the cashier of Nawab Murshid Quli Khan, but the revenue of the province was also deposited with him. Together they established Murshidabad, the new capital of Bengal and sent 20 million rent to Aurangzeb instead of one crore thirty lakhs. In 1715, the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar conferred the title of Seth on Manik Chand. For this, a seal was made by carving Jagat Seth on a large page, which was presented to Fateh Chand in the royal court along with other rare gifts. After this this family came to be known as Jagat Seth. After Manikchand, the reins of the family came in the hands of Fateh Chand, during whose time this family reached the heights.

27/11/2021, 23:46 - History Guruji: nice question
28/11/2021, 00:17 - Vaibhav: Counterfeiting was prevented by various types of government throughout the history of mankind. It's a good question @⁨~Kshitij⁩ sir, but first we should know why did Governments and Kingdoms opposed to such practices?

The answer was because of profit and self gain of the empire, kingdom or the government irrespective of the time period. 

It also weakened the economic status of the empire as the control over economy slipped from the rulers hands into some others hands. If the other one prints it in copies amounts, it would result in inflation or hyperinflation which would weaken the empire both at the political and the world stage.

Now some measures to avoid this were as follows-

1) The ancient kingdoms of China in 14nth century like the Songs and Jins heavily guarded the sources of raw materials. In China, it was the Mulberry Trees. And in other parts of the world including India, the mining industry was checked regularly due to various other reasons including  third party dealings of Iron, Copper, Silver, Gold etc.

2) Under the Delhi Sultanate especially after Allaudin Khalji's economic reforms, the engravings or the Mohar was taken into consideration by the locals while buying and selling goods. But it changed with time as it the counterfeiting was gaining the upper hand in the 17-20th century. The empires heavily monopolized the use of raw materials especially metals for crafting fake currency. People were questioned about the uses while taking the raw materials. 

3) The practice of accounting counterfeiting as treason and severe punishments actually raised terror I the minds of the people in doing anything illegal. The terror and display of the 'traitors' were publicly displayed. It was prevalent in almost the entire world.

The modern techniques and technologies brought new and innovative ways to counterweight counterfeiting. Metal strip detectors, usage of polymer, diffrence in the way of printing and usage of pictures and portraits in bank notes had revolutionized the history of countering counterfeiting.

04/01/2022, 18:45 - Vaibhav: In the immediate aftermath of the war, the troops first secure the land and are placed on the new border. Then it depends on what the Victor would do. Here are some things kings have done from time to time in this situation. 

• Looting and Pillaging 
• Sacking important towns in the conquered areas.
• Wiping out or catching the enemy forces which backed out from the war etc.

Then they either installed thier governers to givern the land or give one of thier trusted allies the land who fought with them despite being from the land or they carve it up.

Then these governers then either implement thier system with force and oppression or continue the system used in the old regime.

These systems helped in collecting taxes. The Governer then picks some officials or old Zamimdars or tax collectors from the Victor's land which could have migrated into the new conquered territories. When these positions are given, these are given the autonomy and a promise of maintainence and support. The main power however lies within the Giverner who is at the top. 

The policy of mixed religion and propagandas is used to manipulate the locals to defect to the Victor's side.

08/01/2022, 20:50 - Vaibhav: The Gulf Ruppee was a currency issued by the Reserve Bank of India for some gulf states. 

This actually was a big relief for both India and the other states as well. Since the Foreign Trade Exchange of India was on its hunt for opportunities since independence, this was a great opportunity for India.

The currency was short lived, I think 7 years or so and India stopped its production in 1966 as the nation's began to develop and use its own currency. By 1970, it ceased to exist in the previously- currency dependent nations. 

It was mostly used by traders and could only be redeemed at Bombay or Mumbai only. There was a body for this redemption purpose as well.

But still it was a boost for the Foreign Trade Exchange who was searching for opportunities for so long. It was a great start for them.

21/01/2022, 23:52 - +91 81601 63689: There are variables to be taken into context, to get the exact date of an idol. Broadly they are-

a) study of art form - elementary / mature (original or inspired or improved)
+
Context of the art (proto or not); as annexure or the prominent one
+
Posture - meditating (mudras)/ fighting (types of weapons- axe or sword? If sword, then what kind of sword? Has there been excavations of such sword in the surrounding areas?)
 +
Paintings, texts etc


b) s&t - if its baked or very well chiseled (refer thermo- luminescence dating technique);  if made of wood (K-Ar / C14  dating).  


c) Archelogy - if its very old and buried - refer dates of surrounding objects (biological or otherwise) & stratification charts (is it T1/T2/T3... ) ; aeolian / pluvial / glacial etc... 

Etc...

Actually, these are all considered simultaneously to get a better idea of an "age"

Case study - You may refer to Ajata or Ellora and that how they changed over a period of time. They have various forms of art (idols, including female figurines ) that shows how it all started and how it ended.

04/03/2022, 18:12 - Harshdeep Sir: "Khan Jahan Lodi was an ethnic Afghan who had been a close confidant of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir and gained increasingly important positions at court. After Prince Khurram (later Emperor Shah-Jahan) rebelled against his father, Jahangir appointed Lodi commander-in-chief of his army, after. He did not support Shah-Jahan as heir and, according to the Padshahnamah text, after many of the Afghan tribes declared allegiance to him following the new Emperor’s accession ‘his brainless head’ became ‘a nest of false and demonic hopes and vain fancies’. In 1629, the former commander fled towards the court of the Nizam Shah in the Deccan but, when Shah-Jahan’s forces closed in, he and his entourage turned north towards the Punjab. They were eventually hunted down and one of his companions, Darya Khan Rohilla, was slain. Khan Jahan escaped but was pursued and eventually killed by Madho Singh on 3 February 1631 at Sihanda in central India. This painting captures the moment that his head was sawn off after the combat."

-Royal Museum, description of Padshahnama
04/03/2022, 18:14 - Harshdeep Sir: Miniature detail-

"All of the action takes place in the foreground: a circle of soldiers surrounding the two who commit the deed. ‘Likeness of the headless’ is written beside Lodi’s face in ink containing gold flecks and, on the sleeve of the soldier crouched over his body, is the inscription shah-jahani, meaning ‘one who owes allegiance to Shah-Jahan’, leaving no doubt as to the imperial nature of the gruesome act. Six other heads are scattered about the painting, including one on a pike and two held by the hair in the clenched fists of soldiers in the foreground – those of Lodi’s son Aziz and Emal. Despite their calm demeanour, not all of the surrounding figures seem able to watch and it is only the grotesque masks decorating the armour of certain individuals to the left and right that appear to react in horror to what is happening. Dressed in a bright orange jama on the right is the Rajput officer Madho Singh, proudly holding the lance with which he fatally struck the Afghan rebel. In the mid-ground, Sayyid Muzaffar Khan of Barha and Abdullah Khan, the leaders of Shah-Jahan’s imperial forces, face each other in a near mirror image. They were well rewarded for their victory, the title Khan-Jahan given to the former as inscribed in the painting on the hilt of his sword. At the apex of the pyramid is a figure looking directly at the viewer with his arms outstretched. He may be Farid, the only son of Lodi to be captured alive, holding his arms up in surrender. He stands directly below a chinar tree, a species brought to India by the Mughals which was often associated with the Timurid dynasty, perhaps a symbol of the absent Emperor. A row of soldiers labelled ‘the world-conquering army of the Second Lord of Conjunction’ appear behind a rocky outcrop in the background."

The artist Abid signed the work and recorded its completion in Agra: ‘work of slave of the court Abid'

16/03/2022, 21:30 - Vaibhav: The Pre-Mughal Architecture  was diverse where the north had Indo-Perisan Architecture, the south brought in influential artists and architects from the Middle East mainly from the Ottoman Empire. This forged into a Indo-Islamic Architecture somewhat diffrent from the architectural marvels of the Delhi Sultanate which pursued the Indo-Persian style.

The Southern part of the Subcontinent mainly under the Vijaynagra Empire and the Bahmani Sultanate. The Bahmani Sultanate went for an open style. 

For instance, the Charminar built is an open structure and an archway which carried Delhi's style and Turkish elements. 

The Vijaynagra Empire and the Gajapatis of Orrisa went for rebuilding the old style pursued by the South Indian Dynasties. Vijaynagra later started trade with the Middle East and this brought about a change. Note that this was before 1527.

•Mughlai Architecture-.

Mughlai Architecture is just an image of the success of its ancestors like the Timurids. Mughlai Architecture is mostly Indo-Persian with some Turkish and minor Central Asian Elements. The main monuments were surrounded by smaller but complex architectures. 

An example is the four pillars at the 4 edges to the centre in the Taj.

29/03/2022, 18:54 - History Guruji: Lest We Forget: On this day in 1884, 13 European nations shamelessly gathered in Berlin to parcel out the African continent like famished school children (on a school trip) haphazardly dividing up a pizza. Great Britain was represented by Sir Edward Malet (Ambassador to the German Empire). The US, the emerging but reluctant superpower, had a delegate - the explorer Henry Morton Stanley. 

In utter disregard and with not a single iota of conscience or concern for the culture or the families of the continent, the map was redrawn and lands claimed. What followed was the systematic scramble and undoing of Africa. Resistance was met with the brutal force of gunpowder. The Herero Massacre was the first genocide of the 20th century: tens of thousands of men, women and children were shot, starved, and tortured to death by German troops as they put down “rebellious” tribes in what is now Namibia. Tens of thousands of defenseless women and children were forced into the Kalahari desert, their wells poisoned and food supplies cut. 

In Uganda, the first election fraud (in favor of Apollo Milton Obote) was masterminded by London. The British governor then, Sir Fredrick Crawford, an honest man to a fault, resigned because he was unwilling to be party to this gerrymandering. This has since become the template for regime survival. Congo and many other African nations have never recovered from this trauma that was orchestrated at Bismarck's official residence on that bleak weekend. 

With the emergence of another domineering superpower, may this history not be lost to us.

02/04/2022, 20:45 - Vaibhav: Under the later reign of Shivaji Sambhaji Raje, we see many upside and downs in the Maratha Economy. This was due to the Mughalai Dakhani expeditions. The Adil Shahis of Bijapur sought to seek aid from the Mughals for thuer fading hegemony in the Konkan Coast where Shivaji had established himself. The Maratha Victories were equally heavy to the Mughals. But here is the thing, Mugals could easily replace loses while the Marathas had to be cautious for every sacrifice. As when the Economy began to drain, mainly due to tensions in Europe between companies and drain of castle wealth by the Imperial Mughlai forces, we witness the rise of the art of Gureelia Warfare. This masterpiece was an effort to use less resources to win against the resourceful. 

But still the issue persisted till King Rajaram came whose reign saw a certain restart in the economy but the real power would take some more time to come.

And this came with the reign of the Peshwas and here we see the reliance on Levied Taxes and Trade coupled with territorial expansion. Thier main sources were Territotial Expansions carried out by Peshwa Baji Rao which lasted till Peshwa Balaji Bajirao and later Madhavrao, though at least for some time. The reliance for Chauth (25% of produce) and Sardeshmukhi (10% of resources). This can also be seen in Maratha afterwar consessions especially with the Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad. 

The Marathas under the Peshwas also encouraged Trade and established trade routes and cities like Allahbad (now Prayagraj), Hoshangabad, Ujjain etc. The routes spread from all the sovereign Maratha Territory and all the Maratha States mainly from Holkar, Scandia and Bhonsle Confederate Territories. While cities like Kalyan, Thane and Surat continued thier flourishing period.

After the 1763, Third Battle of Panipat, the Maratha Economy began to crumble. Many as the Martha's weren't able to finance for the trade. As one's one needs and survival is in danger, all the materialistic distractions seem to dissappear.

This state was fueled by political instability of the Maratha Raj and the somewhat split of the Marathawad Kingdom of Thanjavur.

Still the economy was still not in a dire state but not as good as in the past though. But trade and taxation began to be the centre of Maratha Economy until the British takeover of French, Dutch, Danish, Portugeese holdings. 

Then comes the First Anglo-Maratha war where the Economy was in tatters but the Marathas somehow managed to stay afloat due to the presence of Good leadership. But all things had to end and bit by bit, the sources shortened and so did the economy.
