05/04/2022, 22:44 - Vaibhav: Good Question Sir ji, there are two viewpoints for the answer to this. 

For the people who took it on to lead his republic, they had strong feelings about this new idea. And many of them were rich too of course at the time, and so they certainly commissioned people to do it for them. This is the lesser know part that we find in the western world. It also could be as they were enthusiastic and optimistic about this idea. We can see this from the nature of the Greeks.

But from the viewpoint of the common people and writers, even the literal prospect of copying a document like this is quite absurd, to say the least. Writers especially in Greece, preffered to copy books regarding study, religion and even theology. But Constitution copying enthusiasts could be there. Though the probability to do that is quite less in its own rights. Besides, the locals didn't may much heed to this fancy new ideas. They proffered thier agricultural, herding lives.

Another prospect is that thus constitution attracted the rich and its copies would have a certain demand to be kept to spread this. So there is some little possibility that Journeymen and migratory writers might indulge themselves in such actions. This occurrence was somewhat fair or less popular in Europe. Though I personally doubt the latter 2 but it's always interesting to share this interesting and less talked about viewpoints.

03/05/2022, 14:43 - Vaibhav: This is infact a 19nth century painting depicting a Hindu Temple in Astarkhan, Southern Russia.

This was due to two events in Central Asian History-

• The first is the Pax Mongolica. Since Astarkhan was under the Qipchiq Khanate, merchants from India traded intensively alongside the  Mongol silk route. And since cities like Astarkhan, Isfahan, Nishapur, Tabriz and Baghdad became effective hubs of commerce and cultural exchange, we see some Hindu minorities staying that. And the Qipchiqs were religeously tolerant in thier early reign.

• Our next event, is the Safavid Iran which restarted the Silk Route. Considering Mughal relations with the Safavids, we do have subdivision trade routes too. From Gujrat to Qazvin and then to Isfahan. From there, it can move to other subdivision routes. It's important to note that Astarkhan was still a popular hub for commerce though a reduced one, not to say the least. So we could have Hindu merchants moving to Astarkhan via the affrimentioned route until the Russian Conquest. The Russians under the tolerant Peter the Great granted religious privileges. And since, there wasn't much religious enforcement too, the success rate for maintaining the Hindu Religeous identity turned quite high. They would probably be Vaishnavites and the people responsible for spreading the virtues of Lord Krishna all over Russia today.  This is my opinion on this topic.

I would like to bring some overlooked points while looking at Sikh-Afghan war after Third battle of Panipat, some of the claims that "Abdali suffered great both militarly and financially in the battle which very easily & quickly resulted in the decisive Sikh victory in the war against Afghans" while there are no doubtful thoughts that battle of Panipat did impacted the intensive Sikh-Afghan struggle, in a way that Sikhs were isolated after destruction of Maratha military juggernaut, they didn't had any ally, Marathas as we know were gone (exception- presence in Central India = Malwa), Rajputs were already with Afghans, Jats under Suraj Mal had made friendship agreement with Afghans (Najib) which gave them Agra (Akbarabad). Unlike the 1758 Punjab campaign Sikhs didn't had any allies or coalition to tackle Afghan menace. Further more now on their eastern front was replaced by powerless Mughals and in their position arrived Rohillas under Najib-ud-daulah. Some of the points- Favourable environment for Sikhs Misls, Abdali losing all of his capability of waging any kind of future campaign in India (especially the one aganist Sikhs) after Panipat, Sikhs winning without any much losses, one front war. 

1. Much of the talk about favourable environment has been made that was available to Sikhs however, military coalition wise it wasn't, Marathas and Sikhs who were allied for a common objective of tackling Afghan ambition now after Panipat Marathas were no longer in any capacity capable of linking up with Sikhs in Punjab and waging war as allied coalition or even provide financial assistance to Sikhs aganist Afghans further more Abdali's launching base was already on their western front but now on their eastern front Rohillas appeared then Pahari Rajputs who were north of plain Punjab allied with Afghans immediately thus environment wasn't favourable to Sikhs being surrounded and cut off from any potential ally

2. Much of the picked up point here is that loses of Afghan side after Panipat was so much that Abdali despite decisive victory, lost all of his capability to wage any campaign in India hence the Sikh struggle was quickly over with easy win, first most fact is overlooked here (even in video unfortunately) is that Abdali was able to wage a constructive campaign in India spacially against Sikhs for almost 4 times meaning continuing war from 1761-1768

3. Even more interesting is to note that just like Marathas at Panipat, engagement at kup (1762) resulted in the lose of 25k-30k Sikh combatants and further considering the low number of manpower and resources this was a huge lose to Sikhs but after 6 months they inflicted defeat on Afghan officer Zain khan then in rapid succession aganist Abdali near Amritsar, the Sikhs were able rise up from such lengthy devastating loses and gained ultimate victory which wasn't a easy victory as been portrayed.

4. The look over Sikh-Afghan war has been limited to Afghan invaders coming from west front of Punjab however in 1764 (continuing upto 1770) Sikh-Rohilla struggle begin moreover in 1767 when Abdali was again waging war suppressing Sikhs he linked up with Rohillas on East side in Delhi Subah and Najib sent his favourite son, Zabita Khan with 15k Rohilla troops who joined Abdali's 40k moreover Najib funding Afghan forces 6 lakh rupees every month as expense cost moreover tribute (peshkesh) paid by Jawahar Singh son of late Suraj Mal amounting to 20 Lakh rupees went straight to campaign funding. Despite such odds Sikhs stood in the way of Afghan juggernaut not only securing Punjab (even upto Multan 1771-1780) but also checking any more Afghan invasions

Napoleon Bona­parte created the Banque de France to foster eco­nomic recovery after the strong recession of the revolu­tionary period. This new insti­tution was charged with issuing notes payable to bearer on sight, in return for dis­counting of trade bills. The ori­ginal statutes organised the activ­ities of the Bank, but other com­peting issuing insti­tu­tions remained. Napoleon III, or Louis-Napoléon, original name- Charles-Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, Emperor of France (1852–70). He was the nephew of Napoleon I. He evoked the legend of Napoleon to win the popular vote as president of the Second Republic. Attempting to expand his power, he staged a coup in 1851 and made himself dictator; in 1852, as Napoleon III, he became emperor of the Second Empire. Seeking to reestablish French power, he led France into the Crimean War and helped negotiate the treaty at the Congress of Paris (1856). He sided with Sicily against Austria (1859) and was victorious at the Battle of Solferino. He aided Italy in achieving unity and annexed Savoy and Nice (1860). He promoted liberalized policies within France, which enjoyed prosperity during much of his reign. In the 1860s he gradually introduced political liberalization. He expected material rewards from his “Latin empire” after installing Maximilian as emperor of Mexico (1864–67) but was disappointed. He was defeated in the Franco-Prussian War.

20/05/2022, 10:25 - +91 88272 89921: *In North America*
The boundary between British and French possessions in North America was largely undefined in the 1750s. France had long claimed the entire Mississippi River basin. This was disputed by Britain. In the early 1750s the French began constructing a chain of forts in the Ohio River Valley to assert their claim and shield the Native American population from increasing British influence.

The British settlers along the coast were upset that French troops would now be close to the western borders of their colonies. They felt the French would encourage their tribal allies among the North American natives to attack them. Also, the British settlers wanted access to the fertile land of the Ohio River Valley for the new settlers that were flooding into the British colonies seeking farm land.

The most important French fort planned was intended to occupy a position at "the Forks" where the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers meet to form the Ohio River (present-day Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania). Peaceful British attempts to halt this fort construction were unsuccessful, and the French proceeded to build the fort they named Fort Duquesne. British colonial militia from Virginia accompanied by Chief Tanacharison and small number of Mingo warriors were then sent to drive them out. Led by George Washington, they ambushed a small French force at Jumonville Glen on 28 May 1754 killing ten, including commander Jumonville. The French retaliated by attacking Washington's army at Fort Necessity on 3 July 1754 and forced Washington to surrender. These were the first engagements of what would become the worldwide Seven Years' War.

 *In Europe*
In the War of the Austrian Succession, which lasted from 1740 to 1748, King Frederick II of Prussia, known as Frederick the Great, seized the prosperous province of Silesia from Austria. Empress Maria Theresa of Austria had signed the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 in order to gain time to rebuild her military forces and forge new alliances.

The War of the Austrian Succession had seen the belligerents aligned on a time-honoured basis. France's traditional enemies, Great Britain and Austria, had coalesced just as they had done against Louis XIV. Prussia, the leading anti-Austrian state in Germany, had been supported by France. Neither group, however, found much reason to be satisfied with its partnership: British subsidies to Austria produced nothing of much help to the British, while the British military effort had not saved Silesia for Austria. Prussia, having secured Silesia, came to terms with Austria in disregard of French interests. Even so, France concluded a defensive alliance with Prussia in 1747, and the maintenance of the Anglo-Austrian alignment after 1748 was deemed essential by the Duke of Newcastle, British secretary of state in the ministry of his brother Henry Pelham. The collapse of that system and the aligning of France with Austria and of Great Britain with Prussia constituted what is known as the "diplomatic revolution" or the "reversal of alliances".

In 1756 Austria was making military preparations for war with Prussia and pursuing an alliance with Russia for this purpose. On 2 June 1756, Austria and Russia concluded a defensive alliance that covered their own territory and Poland against attack by Prussia or the Ottoman Empire. They also agreed to a secret clause that promised the restoration of Silesia and the countship of Glatz (now Kłodzko, Poland) to Austria in the event of hostilities with Prussia. Their real desire, however, was to destroy Frederick's power altogether, reducing his sway to his electorate of Brandenburg and giving East Prussia to Poland, an exchange that would be accompanied by the cession of the Polish Duchy of Courland to Russia. Alexey Bestuzhev-Ryumin, grand chancellor of Russia under Empress Elizabeth, was hostile to both France and Prussia, but he could not persuade Austrian statesman Wenzel Anton von Kaunitz to commit to offensive designs against Prussia so long as Prussia was able to rely on French support. The Hanoverian King George II of Great Britain was passionately devoted to his family's continental holdings, but his commitments in Germany were counterbalanced by the demands of the British colonies overseas. If war against France for colonial expansion was to be resumed, then Hanover had to be secured against Franco-Prussian attack. France was very much interested in colonial expansion and was willing to exploit the vulnerability of Hanover in war against Great Britain, but it had no desire to divert forces to Central Europe for Prussia's interest.

French policy was, moreover, complicated by the existence of the Secret du Roi—a system of private diplomacy conducted by King Louis XV. Unbeknownst to his foreign minister, Louis had established a network of agents throughout Europe with the goal of pursuing personal political objectives that were often at odds with France's publicly stated policies. Louis's goals for le Secret du roi included the Polish crown for his kinsman Louis François de Bourbon, Prince of Conti, and the maintenance of Poland, Sweden and Turkey as French allies in opposition to Russian and Austrian interests.

Frederick saw Saxony and Polish west Prussia as potential fields for expansion, but could not expect French support if he started an aggressive war for them. If he joined the French against the British in the hope of annexing Hanover, he might fall victim to an Austro-Russian attack. The hereditary elector of Saxony, Augustus III, was also elective King of Poland as Augustus III, but the two territories were physically separated by Brandenburg and Silesia. Neither state could pose as a great power. Saxony was merely a buffer between Prussia and Austrian Bohemia, whereas Poland, despite its union with the ancient lands of Lithuania, was prey to pro-French and pro-Russian factions. A Prussian scheme for compensating Frederick Augustus with Bohemia in exchange for Saxony obviously presupposed further spoliation of Austria.

In the attempt to satisfy Austria at the time, Britain gave their electoral vote in Hanover for the candidacy of Maria Theresa's son, Joseph II, as the Holy Roman Emperor, much to the dismay of Frederick and Prussia. Not only that, Britain would soon join the Austro-Russian alliance, but complications arose. Britain's basic framework for the alliance itself was to protect Hanover's interests against France. At the same time, Kaunitz kept approaching the French in the hope of establishing just such an alliance with Austria. Not only that, France had no intention to ally with Russia, who, years earlier, had meddled in France's affairs during Austria's succession war. France also saw the dismemberment of Prussia as threatening to the stability of Central Europe.

Years later, Kaunitz kept trying to establish France's alliance with Austria. He tried as hard as he could to avoid Austrian entanglement in Hanover's political affairs, and was even willing to trade Austrian Netherlands for France's aid in recapturing Silesia. Frustrated by this decision and by the Dutch Republic's insistence on neutrality, Britain soon turned to Russia. On 30 September 1755, Britain pledged financial aid to Russia in order to station 50,000 troops on the Livonian-Lithuanian border, so they could defend Britain's interests in Hanover immediately. Besthuzev, assuming the preparation was directed against Prussia, was more than happy to obey the request of the British. Unbeknownst to the other powers, King George II also made overtures to the Prussian king, Frederick, who, fearing the Austro-Russian intentions, was also desirous of a rapprochement with Britain. On 16 January 1756, the Convention of Westminster was signed, whereby Britain and Prussia promised to aid one another; the parties hoped to achieve lasting peace and stability in Europe.

The carefully coded word in the agreement proved no less catalytic for the other European powers. The results were absolute chaos. Empress Elizabeth of Russia was outraged at the duplicity of Britain's position. Not only that, but France was enraged and terrified, by the sudden betrayal of its only ally, Prussia. Austria, particularly Kaunitz, used this situation to their utmost advantage. Now-isolated France was forced to accede to the Austro-Russian alliance or face ruin. Thereafter, on 1 May 1756, the First Treaty of Versailles was signed, in which bothg nations pledged 24,000 troops to defend each other in the case of an attack. This diplomatic revolution proved to be an important cause of the war; although both treaties were ostensibly defensive in nature, the actions of both coalitions made the war virtually inevitable.

In 1798, he established himself at Hansi and carved out an independent kingdom in the wastelands of Haryana. From Hansi, he ruled over Hissar, Hansi, Sirsa and Rohtak. In 1799, he attacked Jind and defeated the combined forces of the chiefs of Patiala, Kaithal, Jind, Ladva and Thanesar and imposed upon them his own terms for friendship.

But soon after he broke the truce and took possession of Fatehabad and pillaged the Sikh territories of Bhavanigarh, Sunam, and Narangval. He invaded Kaithal and Safidon, but was halted at the latter place and defeated. In  1801, he was badly defeated by the Sikhs and Louis Bourquien, a French officer in the service of the Marathas, 
They drove George Thomas to Hansi which was laid under siege. Bourquien asked Thomas to surrender, offering him a position in Daulat Rao Scindia's army.

Thomas refused, vacated Hansi and marched off to Georgegarh. The whole of Bourquien`s army, now reinforced to 20,000 men, came in pursuit of him. Outnumbered by the Maratha forces, Thomas surrendered to Louis Bourquien on 1 January 1802, but was allowed to retire to British territory. En route to Calcutta, he died of a fever on board his pinnace at Berhampore, West Bengal, on 22 August 1802.

On the north lay the Ghaggar river which separates it from the lands under Sikh occupation; the west the country of predatory Bhatti tribes, beyond which lay the deserts of Bikaner. The south was bounded by the Rewari district.”

Thomas ruled over an extent of territory which had formerly contained nearly a thousand towns and villages, and produced an annual revenue of Rs.14,30,000 (1707-50). But the number of the former was now reduced to little more than a quarter, and only yielded Rs.2,86,000 a year.

Besides these, five more Parganas having 151 villages with revenue of Rupee 1,44,000 were held from Marathas as service tenure. Several important towns such as Fatehabad, Hisar, Tohana, Hansi and Bhiwani were included in his territory.

All in all his territory extended 200 kilometres North – south and same length East – West. This 8000 square miles area yielded twice as much revenue as Patiala state which was spread over 3000square miles and yielded annual revenue of 2,50,000.

However winning was comparatively easier part and keeping Haryana under control was more difficult. George Thomas could collect his revenue only by means of a movable column constantly marching about the country.

Consistent performance for over more than 2 millennia 
As per Angus Maddison’s report, if in 1 CE itself, India’s share of world GDP was 30 percent, it implies that that could have happened only in two ways: 

* it would have either risen to that number steadily over the preceding few millennia or 

* it may have declined from an even higher value over the preceding few millennia.

In either case, it means even prior to 1 CE, India was enjoying a high degree of prosperity. 

These reports were further corroborated by the fact that: 

* 2,000 years ago, with its surplus exports to Egypt and earnings  in gold as returns, India was making Roman Egypt bankrupt of its gold reserves. (Records of the Economic History of Greco-Roman World.) 

* the Indian Merchant Navy  had possessed a fleet strength of 40,000 ships during Akbar’s reign and 34,000 ships before the British took over India. (The historical records of the Indian Merchant Navy.) 

* between 1493 and 1930, India had absorbed 14 percent of the world gold production, meaning that it had earned that much export surplus for five centuries continuously.  (The 1934-35 annual report of the Bank of International Settlements [BIS].) 



From the village to the city
The generations of today  have grown with the belief that wealth lies only in the cities, because of their industries and trade. However, a study of the economic history of India shows a stark contrast to the reality of today. Medieval and Ancient India operated in a different mode:

The economic history of India reveals a secret: 

The wealth of the nagars mainly came from trade. The wealth of this land came, not from colonial exploitation but through sustainable internal resource mobilization - proven, local, self governance.

It was the villages and small towns that were prosperous. They were the centers from where prosperity flowed. Prior to the British period, a lot of wealth was generated in the hinterland and the villages mainly due to the prolific practice of agriculture, multiple bountiful harvests and many small-scale industries abounding in every village of the land. This, in turn, supported the nagars, towns and cities of Ancient India. 

The wealth of the nagars mainly came from trade. The wealth of this land came, not from colonial exploitation but through sustainable internal resource mobilization - proven, local, self governance. A very different picture from today’s modern India.

13/07/2022, 17:55 - +91 98154 11257: Also the indian poetry is very rigid ...Indian poetry is also made on a framework called pingal. There are ragas in music likewise there are chands (poetic meters) in indian poetry. A chand is of two types.
One is varnak which Dictates how many letters can there be In a sentence of poetry
The other is matric which dictates how many syllables are meant to be in sentence of poetry
There are "guru" (long syllables) and "laghu" (short syllables) and some meters have to end with a set combination of long and short syllables such as in the chaupai meter the ends of a sentence have to have a long short long combination

13/07/2022, 18:03 - +91 94256 80489: Any number of notes, that are placed together can give out a tune.
However, some combinations do not give out a very 'melodious' listening to the ear.

Eg. A combination of aloo-mater is palatable, while Baingan-chhola is unheard of.
We can make a sabzi of bainga-chhola also, but it might not be as palatable as one would want his food to be.

Ragas work in a similar fashion. They are a set of notes put together in such a way that it sounds melodious. Each raga has it's own manifestation. So by just listening to the 'catch' notes one can identify which raga is being played.

This pattern is laid out for the benefit of the listener, so that he gets the best of experience.

Being 'rigid' is subjective.
Indian classical music gives the player a free hand to improvise on any raga, within set boundaries.
This is unheard of in western classical music, wich is far more 'rigid' as the player HAS to play the composition EXACTLY as it is noted down (or by rote).

Indian classical music can deliver the same raga in new way everytime it is played.

20/07/2022, 19:38 - Harshdeep Sir: <Media omitted>
There were many maps produced in ancient times especially considering Alexander's invasion of India but most of those works are extinct. During Roman empire particularly two large maps were commissioned for common public by first principate Augustus's military commander Agrippa which included India however none of them survived and copies didn't continued for more than a century. Claudius Ptolemy composed treatises (there many though) on geography in 2nd century AD which was copied upto Byzantine era and earliest Manuscript containing map of world (including India) was issued in mid 14th century (1300's). There is another work which was composed in 1152 AD by a Arab geographer Al-idrisi entitled "Nuzhat al-mushtāq fī ikhtirāq al-āfāq" (Book of pleasant journeys into faraway lands) however the copy and classic drawn map survived in a copy of 1557 AD so the original maps drawn in 1152 AD didn't survived. So Claudius Ptolemy's work is only description and map which is earliest however I should inform that if you are looking at earliest map of India then many were produced after Alexander's invasion of (Punjab) India, especially during later Roman Republic or Early Roman empire where we begin to find mention of maps but if you are looking for earliest (available) existing map of India then Claudius Ptolemy is the one. 

(Image) 1300 AD projection of world, highlighted part is India

20/07/2022, 20:30 - Vaibhav: In India, the dry fruits are claimed to be first seen and used and South India, mire specifically in inner Tamil Nadu, and parts of inland Northern Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. The date for its first use is debated but most experts tell it close to about 4rth Milennium BC, close to Dates Cultivation in Mesopotamia. 

Also some records regarding the settlers at the Krishna-Tunghbadra Valley are of 2,500 BCE as proved by excavations in Adichanallur in Tirunelveli.

Then the history in the Sangama Period is mostly based on theories. But it is very sure that in this time only, the Dates first spread from South India to North India. But it's not sure whether the northerners moved to the South or the South migrated to North. The matter is still researched but the forst theory seems much more appropriate.

Then comes the Ancient South Indian period. The 3 Kingdoms- The Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas traded extensively over South Eastern Asia and the middle east. Dry Fruits were extensively traded between India, South East Asia or the Malaya, China and the Middle East. Here the following dry fruits were exchanged-

•  China- Apricots, Peaches 
•Middle East- Peaches, Apricots, Dates
• India- Raisins and possibly Dates.

The conflicts for maritime trade routes, trade interests and relations between the Cholas and the Pandyas was a factor for stagnation in Dry Fruit Trade.

The Mauryans and later the Satvahanas connected the Southern Rasins to the North for either the forst or the second time, but under the reign of Emperor Ashoka, dry fruits spread across Northern and Central India.

23/08/2022, 16:50 - +91 81444 90555: The term 'De-notified Tribes' stands for all those communities which were once notified under the Criminal Tribes Acts, enforced by the British Raj between l87l and I947.
These Acts were repealed by the Independent lndian Government in l952, and these communities were "De-Notified".
Some interesting observations is that there are no criminal tribes in the CNT Act list from today's states of Meghalaya & Nagaland.

Criminal tribes were usually those communities that did not comply with British rules that were imposed to control the population. So Nihangs with their firearms is a good example of how British would have had a much harder time controlling the masses if more communities had retained their martial skills & firearm licenses while remaining under weak administrative control.

Please feel free to add more thoughts on political dimensions to why such communities were targetted

06/09/2022, 19:43 - Harshdeep Sir: *Rise and Fall of Jaat Kingdom between 1753 and 1805*

• M Suraj Mal captured Nuh, Palwal, Sohna and Ballabhgarh from Mughals after battle of Ghasera 1753

• M Suraj Mal captured Alwar in 1756 from Rajputs

• M Suraj Mal captured Agra Fort in 1761 after which areas like Dholpur, Firozabad, Etah, Kasganj, Hathras, Aligarh and Bulandshahr came under his control

• In 1762, Maharaja Suraj Mal captured Rewari, Gurgaon, Jhajjar and Rohtak in Haryana from Mughals

• In 1763, battle of Hindon was fought between Jaats and Mughals in which Maharaja Suraj Mal was shot dead. Later, his son M  Jawahir Singh had to leave territories like Rohtak, Jhajjar, Gurgaon and Hapur.

• In 1769 - 70, Marathas overraned Central G-Y Doab area from Jaats.

• In 1770, Rajputs took back Alwar from Jaats.

• In April 1773 after Marathas went back to Deccan, then Jaats re-conquered Central GY Doab areas.

• Battle of Dankaur (Oct 1773) was fought between M Najaf Khan (Regent of Mughals) and Maharaja Nawal Singh in which latter was defeated and M Najaf Khan captured Aligarh in UP and Ballabhgarh, Nuh and Palwal in Haryana.

• Battle of Barsana (Dec 1773) was fought between M Najaf Khan (regent of Mughals) and Maharaja Nawal Singh in which latter was defeated and M Najaf Khan captured Mathura, Agra, Firozabad, Etah, Kasganj, Hathras and Dholpur.

• So after all this Jaat Kingdom was again restricted to Bharatpur and in 1805 Bharatpur became British Protectorate.

By Taraq Madaan

Bengali forces defeated Burmese forces and installed Min Saw Mon as the ruler of Mrauk U. As a result of the victory, Arakan became a vassal state of the Bengal Sultanate.

1.Prohibition against building new churches, places of worship, monasteries, or a new cell. (Hence it was also forbidden to build new synagogues. A similar law, prohibiting the building of new synagogues, existed in the Byzantines, and was therefore not new for all Jews. It was new for the Christians.)
2.Prohibition against rebuilding destroyed churches, by day or night, in their own neighbourhoods or those situated in Muslim quarters.
3.The places of worship of non-Muslims must be lower in elevation than the lowest mosque in town.
4.The houses of non-Muslims must not be taller in elevation than the houses of Muslims.
5.Prohibition against hanging a cross on the outside of Churches.
6.Muslims should be allowed to enter Churches (for shelter) at any time, both day and night.
7.Obliging the call to prayer by a bell or a kind of Gong (Nakos) to be low in volume.

13.Christians were forbidden to provide cover or shelter for spies.
14.Prohibition against telling a lie about Muslims.

25/09/2022, 22:44 - +91 70509 58010: <Media omitted>
Bagha Jatin . 'Tiger Jatin'  born Jatindranath Mukherjee; 7 December 1879 – 10 September 1915), was an Indian independence activist.

He was the principal leader of the Jugantar party that was the central association of revolutionary independence activists in Bengal


Upon returning to his native village Koya in March 1906, Jatin learned about the disturbing presence of a tiger in the vicinity; while scouting in the nearby jungle, he came across a Royal Bengal tiger and fought hand-to-hand with it. Wounded, he managed to strike with a Small dagger (Khukuri) on the tiger's neck, killing it instantly.The famous surgeon of Calcutta, Suresh Prasad Sarbadhikari, "took upon himself the responsibility for curing ... Jatin, whose whole body had been poisoned by the tiger's nails." Impressed by Jatin's exemplary heroism, Dr. Sarbadhikari published an article about Jatin in the English press. The Government of Bengal awarded him a silver shield with the scene of him killing the tiger engraved on it

12/10/2022, 18:22 - +91 94256 80489: In those times cement concrete had not made it big, and lime concreting was too expensive and time consuming (also meant for very large edifices), hence, Wood, which was the cheapest and easily available material, easy to work on, was used to make buildings.

It served the purpose of being light on the pocket and had a decent life period.
The only drawback was that the material had to be of very good quality to start with.
Proper maintenance was required, but it was the norm in those times to periodically clean and maintain the house.

These structures served the purpose of insulating the inhabitants during peak winters and summers.

With time wood became a scarce and expensive commodity to procure. The rising maintenance costs and better workability of cement concrete made everyone turn towards RCC structures.
In a country like India, RCC is not the best bet when we take climatic conditions into consideration. The rapid urbanization in the wake of western influence has brought in too much of concreting into our cities (and villages alike).

I have seen such houses being auctioned off to scrap dealers (in Maharashtra) and it is very sad to see such fine workmanship go to people who do not understand it's worth.

This new generation was dynamic and eclectic in its adoption of novel identities and practices, whether from western race science or from the Hindu and Christian religious repertoires. There are two theories about the origin of Shenoy or Shenvi.

The Sanskrit word Shrenipati, meaning the leader of the guild, which got converted as Shennivayi in Apabhraṃśa, and later as Shenai or Shenvi in old Konkani.

It is from the Sanskrit word for 96, ṣaṇṇavati (षण्णवति). The significance of the word 96 among Konkanis is that 96 villages formed the core region of Goa. It is said that 96 clans / families of Saraswat Brahmins arrived in Gomantak and settled in one village each.[4] 66 villages were in Sashti region (66 in Sanskrit is ṣaṭ ṣaṣṭi - षट् षष्टि. Sashti became Salcette during the Portuguese rule) and 30 villages were in Tiswadi region.

*Issued by King: SAMUDRAGUPTA (C. 335-375 CE)*
*JAVELIN (Class II Type) with Biruda "Parākramah"*

Description of this Class II type:
*On obverse:* King standing facing and offering oblations to the fire alter from his right hand. Garuda standard on the left.
*King's name "Samudra" (highlighted in purple)* written vertically *in Brahmi script* below his left arm. Holding Javelin from his left hand with the spearhead pointed downwards..

On Reverse: *Goddess Lakshmi seated* on the throne holding cornucopia from her left hand with a halo on her head.
*The biruda (imperial title) on right reads "Parākramah"* *(highlighted in maroon) written vertically in *Brahmi script which means "Powerful".*

Wt. 7.78 gms (aprox), Dia. 20mm (aprox).

In early 4th century A.D. a kingdom rose to power in northern part of Indian sub continent, THE GUPTA EMPIRE.
Chandragupta I became the first Emperor in c. 344 A.D.
*Chandragupta chose Samudragupta as his successor..* Under his rule the empire grew and covered northern to southern part of our country. He is often compared with Nepolean & Alexander III (better known as Alexander the Great).
*Samudragupta was not just a great emperor but was also a lover of arts and is considered as a great poet & musician, that can be seen in the Allahabad Pillar inscription as well as over his coins..*

*One such Extremely Rare specimen is this issue*

14/03/2023, 09:15 - +91 88272 89921: Three main reasons

1) Majority of the Maratha strongholds were very near to the Mughal border, so they needed to expand their further south in case of a future invasion by the Mughals. Their southern territories would act as a backup and could also fuel the war effort. This shows how great a visionary Chhatrapati Shivaji was.

2) The political situation of that times was quite favorable for the Marathas, the Mughals were engaged with the Pashtuns in the North-West and returned with an exhausted army. The once powerful sultanates of Golqanda and Bijapur were greatly weakened and the Hindus started gaining more and more power in the courts. They now wanted an intervention from a powerful and sovereign Hindu ruler.
 
3) The rich and fertile plains of Tamil Nadu and the oppressive government of the Jihadis fueled in the mind of the Chhatrapati, the thoughts of a grand campaign in the south. Thus, we can conclude that there were reasons beyond the political level as well. Chhatrapati Shivaji dreamt of an independent Swaraj for Hindus, and how could he ignore the lands, once ruled by the mighty Vijaynagar and Chola empires.

09/05/2023, 20:52 - +91 88272 89921: Was the infamous invader of Kashmir, Dulācha a Mongol? My research shows the other way round:-

1) Jonarāja, the author who continued Kalhaña's celebrated Rājatarāngīni, has described *two* foreign invasions on Kashmir.

2) The first of these was led by the *Turūska* (Turk) Duwa or Dulācha. Here, he is clearly stated as a Turk, with not a single mention of Mongoloid characteristics.

3) The grand invading army consisted of Mlechha, Turūska and Tajikā troops, that is- Muslims, Turks and Central Asians. This invasion or rather an inroad is commonly assumed and described as a Mongol invasion, from *Central Asia*. But the thing is that the invasion should have happened from Northern Afghanistan and Baltistan? No, the actual invasion happened from the south. The later Muslim historians have attributed the invasion to have occured from *Barāmūla Pass*, that's from western Punjāb and upper Jhelum. So, why would the Mongols, coming from C.Asia attack from the south, instead of the western part of Punjab/southern part of Kashmir?

4) Okay, even if we rule in the probability of the invasion to have happened from the South, by the Mongols from the route of Peshawar, then it's also further stated by Jonarāja that the king, Suhadēvā sent Udhyānadēva to first bribe the invader. But when this attempt failed, then the king fled to nearby Gandāhar or Gandhār (that is eastern Afghanistan). This doesn't make sense that the king fled to the territories of his enemies! That equals to the fact that the invader came from south. The next theory is even more interesting and further proves the fact that the invader was from the south.

5) Jonarāja had identified the invader to be in the service of a great king (Chakrāvārtin) Karmasena. This ruler's name remains obscure in the history of Kashmir, we have no clue who he was. But the very thing that clears the fact who this great ruler could be is that the qualities of the army and ruler, that are mentioned by Jonarāja match that of the Delhi Sultan. He could possibly be Ghiyasūddin Tüghlāq, who launched extensive conquests throughout the Indian Subcontinent to consolidate the Sultanate's hold over the vast regions.

6) The later chronicles state that the invader was heading towards Hindūstān, but got caught in a blizzard while crossing the Būdil pass. They also show his leniency by marching through the passages without much preparation. Thus, it shows that he headed towards the south to give the looted wealth to his overlord, not to invade his country.

10/05/2023, 20:27 - +91 88272 89921: Along the Silk Road, there was an ancient country called Sogdia that comprised today’s Uzebkistan and parts of Tajikistan. Their language Sogdian was part of the Eastern Iranian family of languages and written is Aramaic script. The land is mentioned in Tang dynasty chronicles as well as by Greek writers. They had the usual Central Asian religions of Manichaeism, Nestorianism, and Buddhism. But what is interesting is that, till 8th century, a country that would have the hometowns of both the future Timur (Samarkand) and Babur (Ferghana) would also have an unmistakable influence of Hinduism. This is remarkable considering no Indian text ever claimed ruling these places and Sogdia was outside of Kushan empire as well.

They had cults of 5 Hindu gods: Brahma, Indra, Mahadeva, Vaisravana, Narayana. Being an Iranian people, they identified many of these with Iranian gods such as Veshparkar (Vesh is from Vayush - Avestan for Vayu). But depictions of these Iranian gods were mostly like Hindu gods. Some like Narayana did not have any Iranian cognate.

Shubhneet Kaushik 17/05/23 'मैं नास्तिक क्यों हूँ' का भोजपुरी अनुवाद

साथियो, क्रांतिकारी भगत सिंह के प्रसिद्ध लेख 'मैं नास्तिक क्यों हूँ' का भोजपुरी अनुवाद मैंने किया है। ‘हम नास्तिक काहे बानीं’ शीर्षक से। साथ ही, भोजपुरी अनुवाद के लिए लिखी भूमिका में मैंने क्रांतिकारी आंदोलन से भगत सिंह के जुड़ाव और उनकी विचार-यात्रा की संक्षिप्त चर्चा भी की है। 

आज जन-इतिहासकार लाल बहादुर वर्मा की दूसरी पुण्य-तिथि भी है। इस अनुवाद को आपके बीच रखते हुए मैं लाल बहादुर वर्मा को ज़रूर याद करना चाहूँगा, जो मौलिक लेखन के साथ-साथ अनुवाद की महत्ता को लगातार रेखांकित करते रहे।

यह भोजपुरी अनुवाद कॉपीराइट से मुक्त है। कोई साथी इसे मुद्रित, प्रकाशित या वितरित करना चाहें तो इसके लिए वे स्वतंत्र हैं। मुझे सूचित करेंगे तो अच्छा लगेगा। सोशल मीडिया, ऑनलाइन पोर्टल, वाट्सएप या किसी अन्य माध्यम से भी आप इसे साझा कर सकते हैं। 

पुस्तिका पढ़कर अपनी प्रतिक्रिया दीजिएगा। साथ ही, पुस्तिका की भाषा या अनुवाद को लेकर आपके कोई सुझाव हों तो मुझे ज़रूर बताइएगा।  आप इस लिंक पर डाउनलोड कर सकते हैं :

29/05/2023, 10:31 - +91 88272 89921: In 1783, a child was born in Mundal Guat, Bengal, India, with two fully functional heads. The midwife attending the birth was so horrified by this unusual sight that she impulsively threw the child into a nearby fire. Fortunately, the child survived the incident with minor burns.

Realizing the potential to earn money, the child's parents decided to take him to Calcutta, where people paid to see him due to his extraordinary condition. The two heads of the child exhibited independent actions and reactions. While one head would sleep, the other could be awake. Likewise, one head could cry while the other would display happiness. However, both heads responded differently to certain stimuli; for instance, one head was highly sensitive to light and had poor vision. Nevertheless, they both experienced pain in the same way.

Tragically, when the child turned four years old, his mother left to fetch water from a well, only to return and find the child dead. He had succumbed to a cobra bite.

Today, this condition is well-documented and referred to as craniopagus parasiticus, affecting approximately 2 in every 5 million children. Following the child's passing, his body was examined, revealing that both heads possessed their own brains and blood supplies. Remarkably, the child did not suffer from any other illnesses or ailments during his short life.

The child's skull can now be observed at the Hunterian Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons in London, where it stands as a testament to this extraordinary medical phenomenon.

01/06/2023, 11:55 - Vaibhav: The Cholas had a very complex classification system in their navy that was introduced by Raja Raja Chola I, and later his son. The four main classes were

Dharani- The equivalent of destroyers, used for combat on the sea. They could last up to 3 months, traveled in groups, avoided one to one combat.

Loola- Equivalent to modern day corvettes, used for light combat and escort duties. Not meant for frontal assaults.

Vajra- Equivalent to a modern day frigate, fast attack craft. Mostly sent as reinforcements for a stranded fleet.

Thirisadai- Heavily armored, could engage multiple targets, the battleships of those times. They carried a 400 strong, well trained Marine Corps to board enemy vessels. Their name comes from the fact that they could engaged three vessels of the Dharani class.

Apart from the above, you also had the Royal Yatches, which were

Akramandham- Having the Royal Quarters in the stern.

Neelamandham- Mostly used for carrying ministers, officials for conducting extensive meetings.

Sarpamugam- Having ornamental snake heads, smaller yatches used in rivers mostly.

The other ships and boats used were

Yanthiram- Hybrid kind of ship using sails, oars and paddles.

Kalam- Large vessels with 3 masts, that could travel in any direction.

Punai- Medium sizzed vessels, meant for inland transport.

Patri- Barge kind of vessel, used for goods.

Oodam- Small boat with large oars.

Ambi- Medium sized boat, having one mast and oars.

Toni- Very small boat, used in mostly rocky areas

Credits- Ratnakar Sadasyula

Forest owlets, a critically endangered bird, is found only in India, and nowhere else in the world. The bird was first spotted in the 1880s. After that, for almost 100 years, no one even discussed these birds. 

The history of forest owlets dates back to 1872. It was the time when an Irish officer described forest owlets from Chhattisgarh in Eastern Madhya Pradesh. He thought the owl looked different. Until 1884, seven of these birds were collected from different Indian states. This was to create a distribution record of the forest owlets from a particular region or a time. After that, no one even heard about forest owlets.
19/06/2023, 19:27 - History Guruji: In 1976, Ripley, a well-known ornithologist and author of prominent bird reference books, wrote a paper. In this paper, he listed the possibly extinct birds of India—those birds of which there were no records—and forest owlet was one among such birds. These birds looked similar to the common spotted owlet, and were often mistaken for the same. But these species were different from the spotted owlet.

23/06/2023, 16:38 - +91 88272 89921: So, we can conclude that the Mughals lost Qandahar primarily due to 4 main reasons:

1) Persians had superior fighting experience than the Mughals and their army was constantly upgraded, while the Mughal army remained stagnant for most of the period after the death of Akbar. Majority of the Mughal soldiers found difficult to fight in the cold terrain, as they're accustomed to the warm and mild climate of the plains.

2) Geography and climate played a vital role. Qandahar was better connected to Persia than to India. Also, the Mughals didn't have much experience of fighting in the cold regions. Their heavy military wasn't suitable to repulse raids in mountainous terrain. The difficulties related to logistics and rough terrain also delayed the reinforcements.

3) Weak leadership and indecisiveness on the part of the Mughals contributed greatly to the fall of Qandahar. Jahangir failed to send reinforcements to the city, just like he had done earlier in 1605-06 due to the internal disturbances. Shah Jahan's northwest policy, too failed, as the Mughals had to evacuate Balkh and Badakhshan, and they also lost Qandahar.

4) Heavy expenditure to maintain a large and well-equipped army to garrison the region, which yielded little in return wasn't favored by the Mughal emperors. In short, the revenue was quite less to maintain a huge garrison.

08/08/2023, 19:14 - +91 88272 89921: Maratha Rule in Sindh- I had asked whether the Marathas had ever conquered Sindh a few months ago and was told that it's not the case. However, some information I came across seems to suggest the opposite. 

Sindh during this time period was ruled by the Kalhoro dynasty. Noor Muhammad Kalhoro (1719-1755) was a popular ruler who was followed by his son Muradyab Shah Kalhoro (1755-1757). Noor and Muradyab's reigns seem to have been marked by revolts by some Hindu chiefs who took refuge in the hills bordering Marwar and Jaisalmer. Noor Muhammed himself died near Jaisalmer while fighting some rebels it seems. In 1757, Muradyab was replaced by the Muslim nobles with Ghulam Shah Kalhoro.

The biggest opponents of the Kalhoro's in this time period were the Jarejos of Kutch who claimed ancestry from the Samma dynasty of Sindh. The king in this time was Rao Lakhpatji who seems to have sympathised with the Hindu rebels. In 1757, he is said to have presented the Mughal emperor Alamgir II (1754-59) with Kutchi horses and Gujarat bullocks and received the title of Mirza. In 1758, it is said that he had planned a large invasion of Sindh's capital Thatta and entered into an alliance with the Peshwa and Gaekwad for the same. 

In 1758, Raghoba Dada was in Lahore where he mentions in his 4th May 1758 letter that the king of Sindh (लटी) came to meet him. Some Marathi historians mention that kings of Sindh and Balochistan came to meet Dada without delving into their identity. 

The Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency: Cutch, Palanpur, and Mahi Kantha (1880, Page 142) says that it doesn't seem likely that the planned invasion of Sindh took place. However Sindhi sources (despite being very unclear) seem to suggest that there was a Maratha invasion in 1758-59, in which Ghulam Shah was defeated and driven out (some online biographies claim the same as well). Most importantly J.W. Watson in his History of Gujarat (1876, Page 149) does mention that Damaji Gaekwad sent his deputy Shewakram and the Peshwa's viceroy for Gujarat Sadashiv Ramchandra sent a general Ranchordas to join Lakhpatji in this campaign. Also there are claims from the Sindhi sources that Ghulam Shah along with Ahmed Shah Abdalli invaded India from Sindh in 1760, but was badly routed and lost thousands of men during his harsh retreat to Baluchistan due to scorching heat. According to them, the Marathas repulsed his invasions twice, first one in 1758 and the second one in 1760. But the 1000-1200 Marathas withdrew after getting the news of a terrible defeat at Panipat. Ppl exaggerate the size of forces to be 12,000.

Thereafter, in 1762-63, Ghulam Shah launched a large invasion of Sindh and defeated the new Rao Godji II at the Battle of Jara. In 1765, Ghulam Shah again invaded Sindh and peace was established by marrying off Godji's cousin to Ghulam Shah. 

In this scenario-

1. Is it possible that the King of Sindh who met Dada in Lahore was none other than Rao Lakhpatji? 

2. Is it possible that apart from the Rao's campaign the Marathas separately launched an invasion of Thatta Suba (Sindh) from their base in Multan? After all just like Punjab and Doab the Ahmadiyya Karaar gave them taxation rights to Sindh as well. If so what was the role of Kutch, Marwar, Jaisalmer and Bikaner in this? The Bahawalpur chiefs were in constant warfare with the Marathas in this period. They were regularly raided and forced to pay Chauth. 

3. Ahmed Shah Abdali began his reconquest of Punjab through Southern Punjab (Multan to be specific) and he bestowed upon Ghulam Shah Kalhoro the title of Shah Wardi Khan in this time period as well. It doesn't seem likely that Kalhoro's were present in Panipat so could this title be a reward for defeating the Maratha invasion? Or this could be for successfully conquering Kutch?Or even for trying to invade Sindh in 1760? That means Ahmed Shah Durrani laughed a three frontal invasion of India in 1760. 

4. If an invasion was not attempted then why did Ghulam Shah launch multiple invasions of Kutch until the province completely capitulated and the threat was neutralised? He was so thrilled by his victory that he commissioned a new capital of Hyderabad (in place of Thatta). Kutchi sources seem to follow the bardic template of Padmawat in explaining this scenario talking about a Minister who defected to the Nawab and told him of the beauty of the Rao's sister leading to the invasion.
08/08/2023, 19:17 - +91 88272 89921: Maratha Rule in Kashmir-

In his famous letter of 4th May 1758, Raghoba dada mentions "लटी व जंबूचा राजा व काश्मीर वगैरे तमाम वकील आले आहेत" and then talks about settling matters on this side of Attock for now. 

The king of Jammu who came and consulted with Raghunathrao is usually identified with Raja Ranjit Dev (1728-1780). Historians are silent about the identity of the Kashmiri king who's envoy met with Dada. Is it possible that he was Raja Sukh Jivan Mal (1754-1762)? He was an extremely interesting person and his short rule in Kashmir seems to mirror the Maratha conquest of Northwest India. 

He was a Punjabi Hindu Khatri originally from Gujrat which is now in Pakistani Punjab. Abdali conquered Kashmir in 1753 and Sukh Jivan became the Sahibkar to the new Afghan Governor of Kashmir, Abdullah Khan Kabuli. Kabuli was extremely unpopular and Sukh Jivan effected a coup d'etat and became the Subehdar himself. In 1754 he crowned himself as the King of Kashmir and named a Kashmiri Muslim, Abdul Hassan Banday as his Wazir. Sukh Jivan's army had a mix of Kashmiris, Punjabis/Pahadis and Pashtuns. A lot of court intrigues took place which led to Banday being arrested and replaced by Mir Muqim in 1757 (with vice versa happening in 1758).

In 1758, Sukh Jivan set out to conquer Sialkot but massive revolts broke out against him by Kashmiri Muslims in the valley. This led him to abandoning his campaign and hurrying back to the valley. Soon both his Muslim Diwans also revolted and he appointed a Kashmiri Pandit, Mahananda Dhar, as his Wazir. During this period it is said that Dhar encouraged mass migration of Hindus from outside Kashmir into the valley to cement Sukh Jivan's position. He recruited Hindu soldiers from outside the communities traditionally recruited from and these new recruits were said to be extremely ruthless in dealing with the Muslim rebels (and the Muslim population in general). Cow slaughter was prohibited. A prince from the Janid dynasty of Balkh/Bukhara who had taken refuge in Kashmir tried to assassinate Sukh Jivan as well, due to the very same reasons.

In 1761, Abdali won the Third Battle of Panipat. After settling affairs in Delhi and turning his focus to Punjab, he appointed Nooruddin Khan Bamzai to reconquer Kashmir. In 1762 Sukh Jivan was defeated outside Budgam, captured, blinded and brought to Lahore. There Abdali killed him by trampling him under an elephant. 

This raises the following questions-

1. Did Sukh Jivan's planned invasion of Sialkot have anything to do with Raghunathrao's campaigns in Northwestern India around the same time? Where they timed such so as to enable joining of their forces in Punjab and beyond? It is not clear if the Marathas conquered Sialkot but they definitely conquered Multan, Attock and Peshawar. 

2. Because of the revolt Sukh Jivan had to head back. Is that why he sent his Vakeel to hold talks with Dada? A Punjabi Khatri (like Sukh Jivan) from Lahore named Maujiram Baniya was with Dada during his conquest of Lahore and diplomatic manoeuvring in the region as well. 

3. Was Ranjit Dev also a part of the same campaign of Sukh Jivan? It's not known what were the relations like between Jammu and Kashmir at that point of time. The Jamwals stated that they are from Sialkot and made attempts to invade it even in 47. Jammu is anyways barely 40 kms from Sialkot. 

4. Was Raghoba Dada building up a coalition of Hindus from North Punjab (Potohar-Dogra-Pahadi belt; known as the Hill Rajas or Shivalik Rajas in Sikh sources) to act as the bulwark for Maratha expansion into Punjab and Doab/Rohillkhand? Najibabad depended on trade with Kashmir and the Rohillas consistently tried to conquer the Hill Rajas (if not continuously raid and plunder them). Contrary to the propaganda, Marathas always entered new provinces with the support of important local nobles. These nobles and their descendants retained their power and influence and acted as the support structure for the administration and recruitment of troops for the Marathas in these regions (for eg Nandloi Chaudhary in Malwa, Panna royals in Bundelkhand, Mir Habib in Cuttack, Amar Singh Hada and the Kota royals in Rajputana, Dina Arain in Punjab and so on). 

5. Is it possible that the new Hindu soldiers brought in by Mahananda Dhar were Marathas? Authors like PNK Bamzai and Jia Lal Kilam are silent about this. Some surnames of Karhade Brahmins (like Kher) are found in Kashmiri Pandits as well. Is it possible that they were settled there during his time to prop up Sukh Jivan's rule? A large number of Marathi Brahmins settled in Kumaon, Almora and Garhwal regions back then as well. 

6. Also if it's true that Sukh Jivan was propped up by the Marathas 1758 onwards, then it again raises the question as to what did Abdul Rahim Khan do with the help that Raghunathrao gave him? After all he even had an audience with the Peshwa in Pune! It can be determined that he most probably launched an invasion of Kabul-Qandahar, and even captured some key Afghan cities such as Jalalabad, Kabul etc in the name of the Peshwa

22/08/2023, 22:33 - Harshdeep Sir: Rapid campaigning on base of Religious propaganda was cream of the crop for success of Muslim league. Although Punjabi Muslims had dominating position in Unionist party (this will play as important factor in party's fall), but it promoted communal harmony and equal opportunities to all religious communities (Hindu, Muslim and Sikh) in Punjab. Unionist Party was formed mainly by ‘agriculturalist’ the rural sections of Punjab (peasantry and Zamindars/landlords) , with urban middle class support. Founded by Chaudhary Chhotu Ram and Fazl-i-Hussain both ex INC's, party's leadership landed in hands Sikander Hayat Khan as primier and successor of Fazl-i-Hussain. Sikander Khan understood problem that League may present in future, so he made pact with Jinnah in which notable clause prohibited League from campaigning in Punjab although he promised support aganist Congress and British in return. In 1937 Punjab assembly election League could only win 2 seats out of 175 seats, however underground campaign did started to effect common Muslims in Punjab. 

In 1942 Sikander was successed by Khizr Hayat Khan (Tiwana), the effects of second world war began to effect popularity of Unionist party in Punjab. Pro-recruitment currents in 1940 and 1941, Punjab saw a drastic decline in enrolment in 1942 as well as an increase in desertion. Some recruiting officers employed coercion in the countryside, hurting the Unionist image. Inflation and shortages had the same effect: cloth, cement, sugar and kerosene were ‘virtually unobtainable in the villages’ , and there was also an impression was forming among Punjabi Muslims that "the Hindu and Sikh business class gained the most" from lucrative government contracts for supplies while "small Muslim contractors were nearly squeezed out". Khizr’s situation was made more difficult by directives from New Delhi to requisition, at low prices, Punjab’s wheat for distribution in the rest of India, especially Bengal, which saw a great famine in 1943. Khizr and Glancy (Punjab Governor) both objected, but Linlithgow (viceroy of India) was clear, as he wrote to Glancy, that “the procurement of the necessary surplus wheat from the Punjab is more important than any political considerations [and] any interests of [Punjab’s] ministers”. In 1943 situation became worse when Muslim league started to openly campaign in Punjab, in the name of Islam Jinnah started misinterpret ‘Sikander-Jinnah pact’ of 1937. In negotiation to handle it with Muslim league, Jinnah openly told unionist leader Khizr “Bury this Unionist name, perform it's funeral ceremony” , adding that Khizr was ‘a boy leader’ and Unionists seems to him (Jinnah) ‘traitors’ to the Muslim cause. Khizr complained to Glancy but he refused to give British support to Unionist in any matter related to League. Religious campaigning by League against unionist continued without any halt and reached its zenith. Glancy the governor of Punjab presents Khizr's views and prediction in his letter to General Archibald Wavell, which is worth mentioning here: “He (Khizr) does not himself believe in Pakistan, but he thinks that the Pakistan slogan is bound to gain momentum and that it is likely to be a decisive factor in the next elections. He is convinced that Jinnah will employ Maulvis and Mullahs to work up fanatical feeling and will not hesitate to revert to other still more nefarious methods of attack.”

 In 1945 talks between Jinnah and Unionist leader breakdown, Jinnah was successful in asserting to public that the Muslim League was the sole representative of Muslim opinion, this sparked off damaging exodus of MLAs from the Unionist Party's ranks. The defection became irreplaceable damage as even before elections out of 65 muslim unionist MLA'S 40 switched to league while only 25 remained, but soon great blow was received when party's second premier and founder Chhotu Ram passed away on 9th January, 1945. He was mourned by rural populace, it was him who had worked on ground among workers and supporters of party, he was major leader of Haryana Hindu group and tended to break bone of Congress in Northeast Punjab, in his last days he used to repeat in various newspapers, pamphlets and magazine: “Leave religion to the four corners of the temple, the mosque and the Gurdwara. Release yourselves from the bondage of the Maulvis, the Pandits and the Granthis. Do whatever you feel in observing your religious tenets but keep it strictly outside politics”. Jat farmers came to pay respects to deceased Chhotu Ram at Rohtak declaring, “Humara Raja mar gaye!” (our king is dead). Views and changing mindset of defectors of the party is very important as it was affected by Muslim league, (see snippet presenting one example) thus by arrival of provincial election in 1946, stage was set for disastrous defeat of Unionist party in Punjab.

Punjab a History from Aurangzeb to Mountbatten by Rajmohan Gandhi 

Unionist party and partition of India by Ian Talbot 

Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge History) by J.S. Grewal.

Dr Vikram Sarabhai (12 August 1919 – 30 December 1971), physicist and astronomer, the father of the Indian Space Research Organisation which started as INCOSPAR (Indian National Committee for Space Research), set up under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru in 1962 recognising the need for space research. INCOSPAR grew and became ISRO in 1969, within the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE).

In this public domain NASA photograph dated Sep 18, 1969 :- Dr. Vikram A. Sarabhai, (left) Chairman of the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) and head of India's Department of Atomic Energy and Dr. Thomas O. Paine, NASA Administrator, sign an agreement to cooperate in an unprecedented experiment using a space satellite to bring instructional television programs to some 5,000 Indian villages.

20/10/2023, 20:05 - +91 88272 89921: Germany might have not only avoided total defeat at the hands of the Red Army, but even might have achieved a measure of victory against her much larger and more powerful Soviet adversary, which was over forty times larger than Germany at its greatest extent.

1) Don’t invade Yugoslavia and Greece in April 1941.

In actual history, Yugoslavia agreed to join the Axis powers in late April 1941 but days later a coup brought new leadership to power more sympathetic to the Allies. While the new Yugoslav leaders promised the Germans to remain aligned with the Axis as previously agreed while remaining neutral in the war, Hitler viewed the coup as a personal insult and vowed to make Yugoslavia pay, diverting German Panzer divisions from Poland and Romania to invade Yugoslavia and Greece. This ended up delaying the planned German invasion of USSR by five and a half crucial weeks from May 15 to June 22, 1941. In retrospect, there was no military necessity for Hitler to invade Yugoslavia in April 1941. He could have merely sent a few German infantry divisions to reinforce Albania to prevent it from being overrun by Greek troops but he feared potential British reinforcements in Greece, which could threaten his southern European flank. Of course, had Britain and France not still been at war with Germany, it is unlikely that Italy would have invaded Greece in 1940–1941 and risked a British Declaration of War so in that case Operation Barbarossa could have kicked off on May 15, 1941 as originally planned, greatly increasing the chances of a German capture of Moscow in 1941. Combined with Hitler’s subsequent decision to divert his two central Panzer Armies to capture Soviet armies on their northern and southern flanks, this five and a half week delay to the start time of Operation Barbarossa proved fatal to German prospects for victory in the war. Even if Hitler hadn’t pursued a Moscow-first military strategy as his generals wisely advised, invading Russia five and a half weeks earlier might well have been sufficient to enable the Germans to capture Moscow by November 1941, albeit at considerable cost in men and material.


Don’t halt the advance on Moscow of the two Panzergruppen (tank armies) of Army Group Center for two crucial months.

While many historians view the German invasion of the Soviet Union on June 22, 1941 as Hitler’s biggest blunder, evidence from Soviet archives uncovered following the Soviet collapse in 1991 suggests it was successful in preventing a Soviet invasion of Poland and Romania, which had been planned for July 1941. As it turned out, Hitler was correct in his assessment that his invasion of the Soviet Union was necessary as a preemptive attack against Soviets who were planning to attack Germany. In preparation for his planned invasion of Europe, Stalin had, between August 1939 and June 1941, overseen a massive military buildup of the Red Army increasing its total active-duty manpower from 1.5 million to 5.5 million. This expansion more than doubled their total numbers of divisions from 120 to 303 divisions including an increase in the number of Soviet tank divisions from from zero to sixty-one tank divisions as opposed to only twenty total Panzer divisions available in the German Army at the time of Operation Barbarossa. By June 1941, the Red Army boasted seven times more tanks and four times more combat aircraft than invading German forces. The first objective of this planned Soviet invasion of Europe was to occupy Romania to cut off Germany from its access to Romanian oil fields to immobilize the German armed forces and force their capitulation. Then after conquering Berlin and forcing a German surrender, the Red Army was to occupy all of continental Europe to the English Channel, which noted British author, Anthony Beevor, states that Stalin seriously considered doing at the end of the war as well. Viewed in this light, Operation Barbarossa was not a mistake at all but rather an operation which succeeded in destroying the over 20,000 Soviet tanks and thousands of combat aircraft concentrated at the border to invade German territory and postponed the Red Army subjugation of Germany and Europe by nearly four years. Soviet defector, Viktor Suvorov in his groundbreaking book Chief Culprit goes so far as to credit Hitler’s invasion of the Soviet Union as saving Western Europe from being conquered by the Red Army.

Rather, Hitler’s biggest mistake with regards to his war against the Soviet Union was his decision in early August 1941 to divert the two Panzer Armies of Army Group Center to help Army Group North and Army Group South to overrun and encircle Soviet armies on the flanks of its advance resulting in a two month delay in advancing on Moscow when the Soviet capitol was open for the taking. If Hitler had pursued a Moscow first strategy, he could have captured Moscow by the end of August or early September at the latest. He might even have pushed the Red Army back to the Archangel Volga Astrakhan line by October 1941 or by summer 1942 forcing Stalin to accept an armistice recognizing most of Germany’s hard won gains. In his excellent book Hitler’s Panzers East, R.H.S. Stolfi estimated that would have taken away up to 45 percent of the Soviet industrial base and up to 42 percent of her population making it extremely difficult for the Soviets to recover and take back lost territory. While the Soviets could have relocated many of their industries east of the Urals as in actual history, their industrial production would have been much more crippled than it was in actual history without U.S.-UK military industrial assistance. Had the Germans captured Moscow before winter 1941 and held it through the Soviet winter late-1941, early-1942 counteroffensive, Stalin might have requested an armistice on terms much more favorable to Germany than the ones he offered in actual history. Those terms might have included the transfer of much, if not all, of the oil-rich Caucasus region to Germany in exchange for the return of their all-important capitol city to Soviet control. With the Soviets so gravely weakened, Japan likely would have joined the fight to take their share of the spoils and occupy Eastern Siberia as Japanese Army generals had wanted to do all along. Thus, if Hitler had allowed his generals to capture Moscow first, the Germans likely have won the war.

2) Manufacture three million thick winter coats and other winter clothing for the German army before Invading the Soviet Union.

Due to Hitler’s rosy predictions for a swift Soviet collapse and an end to the war in the East by December 1941, Germany failed to produce winter clothing for his invading troops. According to some accounts, as many as 90 percent of all German casualties from November 1941 to March 1942, totaling several hundred thousands, were due to frostbite. Only in late December 1941 did the Nazi leadership admit their mistake and urgently collect as much winter gear from German civilians to send to German troops as possible.

3) Allow national independence and self-rule for all of the Soviet territories liberated by German forces.


Perhaps the biggest key to winning their war against the Soviet Union (other than not fighting the United States and the UK, of course) was for the Germans to not only be seen as liberators from Soviet Communist control, as they initially were when they invaded the Soviet Union, but to actually be liberators from Soviet Communist oppression. The Germans should have used nationalism to rally the people of Belarus, Ukraine and the Baltic States to fight not for the Germans or against Stalin but rather to liberate their own countries from Soviet captivity. They should have allowed self-rule for all of these liberated nations just as Imperial Germany had granted them after defeating the Russian Empire in March 1918 as part of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. In actual history, the Germans captured 5.6 million Soviet troops and captured Red Army Lieutenant General Vlasov offered to lead a Russian Liberation Army to help fight the Soviets while other leaders offered to lead Ukrainian and Cossack Liberation Armies but Hitler would not allow them to be used in combat on the Eastern Front, believing them to be unreliable. If the Germans had treated the citizens of liberated Soviet territories and Soviet Prisoners of War (POW’s) fairly, millions of additional captured Soviet soldiers might have volunteered to fight on the German side. As it turned out, Stalin ended up using the nationalism of Ukraine and other Soviet republics to defeat the Germans instead of the other way around which represented a major missed opportunity for Germany that helped ensure they lost the war.

4) Accept one of Stalin’s offers for an armistice.

After Germany invaded the Soviet Union, they quickly discovered the Soviets had thousands more tanks and a couple hundred more divisions than the Germans had realized before the war. Hitler himself is reported to have remarked that if he had realized how many tanks the Soviets had before the war, he would never have invaded the Soviet Union. However, after the invasion began, he should have realized that the best hope for Germany had they failed to capture Moscow in 1941 or 1942 and achieving his objectives of reaching the Archangel-Volga-Astrakhan line was no longer achievable, was to have concluded a negotiated peace with Stalin ending the war with limited German gains. In actual history, Stalin made a series of peace offers from 1941–1944. The first in July 1941 offered to cede the Baltics, Ukraine (presumably including the Crimean peninsula which was not then part of Ukraine) to Germany. The second in May 1942 added Belarus to sweeten the pot. Stalin’s third peace offer in May 1943 was a proposed ceasefire along the Soviet Union’s 1938 borders which would have effectively reversed the Hitler-Stalin Pact, while leaving the Germans in control of the Baltic states, eastern Finland, the eastern half of Poland and northeastern Romania all of which had been annexed by the Soviets from 1939–1940. This is the only peace offer that Stalin might have been willing to honor long-term. Had Hitler conquered the Caucasus region or more plausibly captured Moscow and ceded it back to Stalin in exchange for the oil rich Caucasus, the Turks would have likely joined the Axis given his promises to turn over the Soviet Caucasus republics (which had briefly won their independence following the signing of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918) to Turkish control following his planned victory over the Soviet Union. 

The apparent rationales behind Stalin’s armistice proposals was to wait until the Western Allies had opened up a Second Front or until Hitler had demobilized and/or redeployed his forces from the Eastern front (as the historical record indicates he planned to) as well as to buy time for the Red Army to rebuild its forces before reinitiating hostilities. At the very least, Hitler’s acceptance of one of Stalin’s peace offers might have served to substantially delay the defeat of Nazi Germany or else potentially enable the Western Allies to occupy all of Germany before the Soviets did, preventing it from being divided into West and East Germany as in actual history.

The reason that Hitler failed to avail himself of this opportunity to end the war with the Soviet Union on favorable terms to Germany is that he deluded himself into believing the German Army could successfully conquer Soviet territories far beyond the German gains of World War One instead of accepting more realistic and achievable gains and objectives. Even in June 1943 when Hitler had given up any plans for further offensives, had ordered the construction of a defensive line in the east and sent his foreign minister to meet with his Soviet counterpart to try to negotiate a peace agreement with the Soviets, he still refused the Soviet peace offer. In retrospect, the wisest thing Germany could have done would have been to complete their encirclements of Soviet forces and/or capture Moscow first and then negotiate a Second Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Stalin beginning in early October 1941 after they succeeded in capturing or destroying the vast majority or the Red Army’s tanks and combat aircraft. Then the Germans could have constructed a fortified defense line to protect their hard-won gains.

21/11/2023, 22:57 - +91 88272 89921: *_Polish Lithuanian Commonwealth – A Failed Concept*_ 

There is a prevalent theory – India stopped every invader because it’s politically fragmented and it’s culture and religion are that tuned that they are ready to accept every kind of thought into it’s socio-religious structure. And when India was invaded, because of it’s political disunity, the invader had to fight for every inch of land only to lose his life force in due course of time and get assimilated. Nothing can be a better example for that than the Islamic conquest of India.

The first wave, the Arabs, was stopped at Bagram and Qandahar. The second wave, the Ghaznavids, reached Yamuna but was beaten back. The next wave, the Delhi Sultanate, wave had to reconquer all lands and conquered all territory the far South. The fourth wave, Mughals, had to reconquer everything which the earlier waves conquered. By the time the Mughal wave reached Tungabhadra, it became a spent force. Had there been a single empire and a single decisive encounter as like what happened at Panipat 1556, what would have been the fate of India?

Why is this relevant to the title of the article? Because Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth is exactly opposite to what happened in India. And neither of them are entities of note after Russian advances starting from 1500s.

By the time of Mongol Invasions, Poland, one of the main kingdoms of the North was territorially fragmented and didn’t present a serious challenge. All it could do was some of the fragments joining forces and presenting a combined front. Lithuania, on the other hand, was the last pagan outpost in the region and it’s existence invited the Church to launch crusades against Lithuanians – crusades which ended with the eventual result – conversion of Lithuania to Christianity.

Lithuania was facing two problems – the crusader armies in the north led by the Teutonic Knights and the flux in Russia on the other. Approximately at the time of Mongol invasions when Russia was shattered, Lithuania became a nation state. Hemmed by Christian countries from all sides – Teutonic Knights in the North, Poland in the West and Russia in the East, it had to maintain a balance between Paganism and the two flavours of Christianity. It had no option but to be aggressive and use every opportunity to assert it’s position. The Mongol invasions was a welcome note for them as they used the power vacuum to strengthen their position advancing till Kiev and having Novgorod, Bryansk, Pskov and other areas under it’s influence. But, the Bubonic Plague undid this delicate balance.

The Bubonic Plague and the subsequent civil war in the Horde broke the power of Golden Horde and propelled Moscow as the main power in the North. Within a century, one would see Moscow unifying Russia and becoming powerful enough to threaten Lithuania.

Jogaila’s lust for power in Lithuania soon pushed a powerful and literally unbeatable Lithuania into a Civil War. This was a direct contributor to the rise of Russia – with Lithuanians fighting all the area from Vilinus to Novgorod and Kiev, it’s but natural someone will use it to it’s advantage. Providence!! Both Golden Horde and Lithuania collapsed at the same time and were unable to stop the rise of Moscow.

Jogaila received two proposals for marriage – the daughter of Dmitry of Moscow and Jadwiga, the Queen of Poland. Had Lithuania been united, such an insult to it’s national memory would have happened – as either of the marriages required the groom to convert to the religion of the bride. Everyone had their reasons for the alliance –

Jogaila’s marriage with Moscow will eventually lead to open rupture with Moscow due to clashing interests as is seen with his cousin Vytautas in due course of time; Jogaila needed a powerful backing against both the Teutonic Knights and Vytautas; Poland wanted a way to stop the raids from Lithuania and protection of it’s Western borders; Moscow wanted support against the Golden Horde.

And thus formed the Polish-Lithuanian Union which in due course of time became Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the largest kingdom in Europe. But, something went wrong. It was not an alliance of resource pooling, it was an alliance of problem outsourcing. Poland wanted Jogila to contain the Germans and Jogila wanted Poland to contain the Teutonic Knights and help him in his civil war.

The Union was actually a success – though Jogila had to accept the rule of Vytautas in Lithuania as his subordinate but de facto independent, the combined forces soon propelled the Union into a great local power. But, in it’s strength lay it’s weakness. An expansionist Russia on one side and an expansioninst Austria on the other – and Ottomans replacing the Golden Horde as the Lord of the Steppes and the suzerain of the Balkans, and with the effort put to subdue it’s hostile conquests, the Union saw it’s power erode in no time. Within 150 years, the cracks on it’s mask was visible. While the Union was formed in 1387, by the time of Vasily III(1502-1533), the writing was on the wall. The chaos after the death of Ivan the Terrible gave them a breather but by the time of Alexei(1645-1676), it was a matter of time the Union would have been consumed by it’s neighbours to maintain a balance of power. Without it’s intervention, the Commonwealth was partitioned by it’s neighbours starting from 1772 and by 1792, the Commonwealth ceased to exist.


Why did this happen? The fundamental reason, one would note, is the Union was created to tackle the enemies on multiple fronts – and it failed massively on that count. Neither was it able to stop Austria nor was it able to stop Russia and had the two entities not been united, it would have been more probable that they would be left independent to maintain a balance of power.
